speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not exactly an equal relationship because the doctor has far more information and expertise than the patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We call this information asymmetry in favour of the doctor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is why the patient-doctor relationship must be undergirded, supported and have its foundations in trust – trust between the patient and the doctor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The patient has to be able to trust that the doctor is doing his best for him; and to the doctor, the interests of the patient must be paramount at all times.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Unfortunately, there will be instances where a doctor might fall short of what is expected of him and the doctor's conduct has to be looked at, and if necessary, sanctions might be imposed on the doctor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In such a situation, a doctor has to be able to trust the system that regulates the medical profession.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He has to be certain as to the standards by which he is to be judged, able to put faith in a system that will be fair, transparent and also produce consistent outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The importance of trust in both contexts cannot be overstated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For patients, the quality of the doctor-patient relationship really has a direct impact on the quality of care and, of course, the outcome of care.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Where that relationship is strong, then patients are more willing and more open to confide in the doctors, and that itself enhances the quality of the diagnosis and the quality of the outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This in turn also allows the doctor freely to focus on the patient's needs, communicate information about the disease or condition and options for treatment honestly, openly and really without the spectre of having to look over his shoulders each time a patient walks into his clinic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, in my view, enhances decision-making and outcomes for the patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For doctors, where the disciplinary system does not effectively and also consistently enforce the profession's standards, they face uncertainty and unnecessary stress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To cope with this, doctors may feel pressured to adopt defensive practices that they think will best protect themselves, not enhance the patient's outcome but protect themselves.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And even in doing so, they might become less effective in serving the needs of their patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have seen and I will show later on in my speech some examples, both here in Singapore as well as elsewhere in the world of such practices proceeding and then undermining the quality of care given to patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over time, these practices erode the trust of the patient and of course undermine the doctor-patient relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That has not changed, and the high ethical standards that are found within the medical profession must be maintained and the patient must know that he receives the best possible treatment, each time and every time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In recent years, however, the relationships of trust that underpin our healthcare eco-system has been called into question, following several well publicised medico-legal cases from the Singapore Medical Council or SMC Disciplinary Tribunals or DTs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was on the basis that he had failed to advise the patient on the risk of possible complications of a steroid injection, some of which subsequently manifested in the patient at hand.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many doctors took the view that the sentence and conviction by the DT were unwarranted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It set an unreasonable standard as to how much information should be given to a patient in order to meet the standard and what that standard might itself be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And many doctors felt that even if there was a lapse in standard in this case, whether it was of sufficient gravamen so as to amount to professional misconduct.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Questions arose as to whether this case ought even have gone to the DT in the first place, let alone result in a conviction with a sentence that attracted the highest possible fine under our legislation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court observed that in Dr Lim's case, it was a "one-off failing committed in the course of a routine procedure", labelling the conviction in fairly strong words, a "miscarriage of justice".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is a very serious indictment on the system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Chief Justice's observations in Dr Lim's case were correct and timely, and served to restore some faith in the outcomes, and of course, also in the system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But members will also recall that shortly after Dr Lim's case, another decision by the SMC DT – this time, in Dr Soo Shuenn Chiang's case – gave rise to some further disquiet amongst the medical profession.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This case also had to be subsequently overturned by the Court of Three Judges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the wake of these cases, there was a significant disquiet within the medical fraternity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many doctors grew uncertain as to what might be required of them when they saw a patient, advised the patient, took informed consent as well as they had also serious concerns as to whether the rigour of the SMC system was sufficient to see through the cases to get a clear, consistent and certain outcome.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And whenever disciplinary outcomes diverge from well-established practices by doctors on patient care within the medical community, uncertainty follows.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Doctors start to question their own judgement as to how much information is going to be enough to care for the patient, and there is the constant worry of whether this patient will make a complaint, and what will happen to the adjudication of that complaint.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I should add the fact that the cases, particularly in those two that I have mentioned and others, have taken an extraordinarily long period of time to be dealt with from the time a complaint was first made, to when the DT resolved the case, has also added frustration, not just for doctors, but also to complainants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this issue has arisen several times on several occasions over the last, I believe, at least a decade, before the Courts, resulting in many cases where the Courts have felt that they had to intervene to reduce the sentence on otherwise recalcitrant doctors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is also an indictment on the system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was done in the period just after Dr Lim Lian Arn's case, the DT's decision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, fewer doctors were prepared to offer the treatment, and when they did, it became more expensive for the patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, there are also accounts from the ground, from the doctors themselves, doctors whom we met – myself with my colleagues at MOH when I was there – with the work group that was appointed by MOH.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We heard, for example, anecdotal accounts of doctors seeking to give patients voluminous amounts of information about all forms of possible risks from the textbooks and alternatives for the procedure, resulting in what the Courts regard as an "information dump" on the patient – a lot more information but really with a lot less understanding.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When the work group – that was appointed by MOH to review the taking of informed consent and to study the SMC disciplinary procedure – discussed the issue at many town halls – and there were many open town halls that took place, both in the private hospitals and in the public hospitals – there was a very clear, palpable sense that doctors grew uncertain of the standards that were expected of them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They were spending less time on patient-focused information and instead, providing information in a manner that they themselves judged would best absolve themselves of liability should the patient complain.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court has – and the lawyers amongst us will know – on numerous occasions said that a doctor does not discharge his obligation to the patient by simply giving information without really trying to solicit understanding.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is not the way to take informed consent, but yet, we have seen numerous accounts of this take place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Beyond our shores, the experiences of other jurisdictions also serve as a warning to what might come if we do not take steps to address these issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This journal was published, taking sensing and surveying statistics from the same jurisdiction where the Montgomery test on informed consent was framed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2001, Minister Shanmugam – at that time when he was a practising lawyer – gave the Singapore Medical Association or SMA Lecture that year entitled "Testing the Bolam Test".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was given at a time when there was a discussion after a landmark decision in the High Court about what the relevant standard of care ought to be when taking informed consent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At that time, like now, the issue arose because of a judicial decision on how informed consent ought to be assessed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These issues, almost two decades ago, are quite the same and also about what to do with the legal standard for informed consent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are also the issues identified by the work group today and it is clear that there is an urgent need to now address these issues swiftly and also decisively.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Minister Gan Kim Yong made a Ministerial Statement in April last year outlining the steps that MOH would take to address these issues and one of them was to appoint a work group.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He gave them a clean canvas and told them in these terms: to leave no stone unturned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Start from a blank canvas, go out and consult with as many as you can, take the time, study it, understand the concerns and make the recommendations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It comprised doctors from various disciplines and also looking at having the composition, came from across a spectrum of different seniority of doctors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It also included the heads of the major medical professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It also comprised lawyers with significant medico-legal experience as well as laypersons with expertise in various fields.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was chaired by a medical director of a national specialty centre as well as a senior counsel.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In formulating its recommendations, the work group consulted extensively with relevant stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They held about 40 town halls and engagement sessions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They went to see the SMC itself; past and present members of the Complaints Committee and the Disciplinary Tribunal; the medical professional bodies, of which there are three and they represent the vast majority of doctors in Singapore; patient advocacy groups to ensure that in scoping the test, one does not also ignore the interests of the patient, which is paramount, as I have mentioned; insurers, who have a relevant role to play in rising healthcare costs and in ensuring that we continue to maintain a cap on where these costs are going; and of course also the lawyers, both on the prosecution and on the defense side in medico-legal cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a very, very broad and extensive range of sessions that they had.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The sessions were a very effective platform for the work group to listen to a wide range of views.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What was obvious was that there was a consistent theme in the call for change, not just in relation to the prevailing legal and ethical requirements but really also in the manner in which the disciplinary process was being conducted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was quite clear that there was an urgent need to restore trust in the system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would say to Members that the broad range and depth of the consultation itself by the work group lends weight to the observations and recommendations which they have made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Starting from a clean canvas, the work group formulated preliminary recommendations from the early feedback they received.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These were then re-presented back to the doctors in different town halls, the medical professional bodies and other groups, and the stakeholders for further views, fine-tuning and testing before they finalise those recommendations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They really kept coming at town halls, meetings, through emails and even on social media.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you talk to the work group members, they will tell you that they really lived and breathed the topic for a good nine months before they produced the report.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Since accepting the work group's recommendations in December 2019, what have we done?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Before coming to the Parliament with these two Bills, we have already implemented some of the changes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those that do not require legislative change – for example,	the enhanced training to ensure that there is quality of personnel across the spectrum of tribunals – has started.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Internally, the SMC has devoted separate and additional resources to clear the existing backlog because Members will know that if and when this Bill is passed, this process and procedure will apply to new cases but not to the existing ones, which are to be resolved under the old regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other aspects, such as the enhanced use of meditation, that has also been promoted to the extent possible, even within the current framework and rubric.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For other changes, we have needed to come to the Parliament for legislative changes to provide for the establishment of the required structures and to reform the process and procedures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will also – apart from what the work group has recommended – propose to include some additional amendments, some related and some fresher ones, to enhance the workflow and to streamline and strengthen the disciplinary process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some of these amendments arise from an earlier review of the SMC process that the SMC had itself commissioned independent of the commencement of the work by the work group.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first is to set a clear standard for healthcare professionals' duty in giving medical advice to their patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On this, Members will note what I have said earlier about there being a lack of clarity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the doctors themselves have that uncertainty, that lends itself to an outcome that is uncertain and in the longer term, leading to defensive practices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clarity, certainty and consistency will be driving principles behind these amendments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill seeks to legislate the standard of care that healthcare professionals have to meet in giving medical advice to their patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For brevity, I will in this speech refer to this as the "duty to advise".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To understand the background and context to these amendments, it would be useful to quickly set out the current legal standard.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Prior to 2017, whether a doctor had met the requisite standard of care in the duty to advise or not was assessed by reference to the practices and opinions of a responsible body of his peers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is called the "responsible body of medical opinion".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some might know it as the Bolam-Bolitho Test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will refer to this 2017 decision as the "Hii Chii Kok test".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court assesses what is relevant and material information from the perspective of the particular patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Hii Chii Kok Test was borne out of the observation that the Bolam-Bolitho Test did not sufficiently give effect to the principle of patient autonomy and that the previous test was regarded as too "doctor-centric".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While undoubtedly well-intentioned, this test in Hii Chii Kok has led to some uncertainty amongst doctors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The work group, in particular, found that many doctors perceived the Hii Chii Kok test as bringing in an element of variability and hence uncertainty as to what each patient might want to know, since what is relevant and material is said to be assessed from the patient's perspective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The test in Hii Chii Kok seeks to strike a balance but the way in which it is articulated has given rise to these uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At paragraph 13 of its report, the work group stated, "While some doctors understand how the test is to be applied, many others have expressed confusion and anxiety about what exactly they are now required to do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some doctors have even candidly admitted that they now practice defensively just to be sure." The work group found that doctors became unsure of how to advise patients in a manner that meets the standard of care, especially so given the realities of practice where doctors see a large number of patients across a wide spectrum on a given day.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add that much of this is likely to be a perceived uncertainty, as I said earlier and as the work group has also found, but perceived or otherwise, this leads to a course of conduct to guard against that perception.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the face of this perceived uncertainty, some doctors have started to adopt defensive practices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In one such engagement, a senior consultant specialist in private practice shared that this doctor took as long as 30 minutes to explain a procedure to patients, not necessarily with the end outcome of ensuring that the patients would come away with it with more information or more understanding but really out of an abundance of caution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This doctor presented this view in a town hall that had close to 250 doctors present.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As the work group put it in their report, "Patients are not necessarily better informed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the contrary, we have received feedback that they are now increasingly inundated with information and are none the wiser." Some doctors have become more reluctant to guide their patients’ decision-making, worrying that they may be accused of paternalism in doing so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Others, such as general practitioners – and we have heard one example earlier in the statistics – have decided not to offer certain treatments altogether.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They opt to refer their patients to specialists instead, for fear of complaints being made against them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these, as Members appreciate, are worrying developments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They threaten patient safety, they undermine the doctor-patient relationship, they make it less cost effective and overall, a weaker system for all.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Another subtle but perhaps understated state of affairs is that the current system is premised on a dichotomy that one has to choose: one has to be either patient-centric or doctor-centric, rendering the patient and doctor constantly pitted against one another in a zero-sum game.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One which acknowledges the reality that doctor and patient are, in fact, on the same side, working towards the same outcome: the good health and recovery of the patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And striving to create an environment where doctors feel safe to give advice to allow a patient to make that judgement himself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But at the same time, creating an environment where the patient knows that he is entitled to ask any question he wants in that consultation, and the doctor has to give due regard to it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for example, information about a procedure that a patient specifically asked for must be provided to the patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this is irrespective of whether some other patient might have wanted it or some other patient might have regarded it as material or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This gives primacy to what might be of concern to the patient at hand – the patient in front of the doctor – recognising that no two patients and no two consultations are identical.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, however, the test will uphold the principle of self-regulation in the medical profession, by providing that regard should be had to what peer healthcare professionals say as to the appropriate standard of care in giving a patient information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is the peer review standard, which I had mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Courts will continue to have oversight, by ensuring that the views of peer healthcare professionals pass muster when it comes to logic and reasonableness.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In concept, this is not a fundamental shift in direction – the underlying principles would be familiar to doctors, to lawyers alike and they are ones which are currently established in law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, we agree with the work group that the way in which the test is articulated best strikes the appropriate balance between the principles of self-regulation and patient autonomy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In Australia, the law of negligence, including its application to professionals such as healthcare professionals, had already departed from the English common law in some significant way in Rogers v Whitaker.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It has been subsequently codified in various Australian states through legislation on civil liability, following a review on the law of negligence by an expert panel in 2002.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, Queensland’s Civil Liability Act and Victoria’s Victorian Wrongs Act prescribe a general standard of care for professionals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Section 21 of the Queensland statute, in particular, sets out the scope of a doctor’s duty to warn a patient of risks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We call this, in short, the “peer professional opinion”.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These two conditions incorporate the same legal principles that were used to assess healthcare professionals’ conduct using the Bolam-Bolitho Test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To be clear, this does not change the burden of proof for civil claims in medical negligence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As before, a claimant patient continues to have the legal burden of proving that the healthcare professional has not met the standard of care in providing medical advice to him.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This statutory test also does not change the test for medical diagnosis and treatment, both of which continue to be governed by the existing legal test in the common law that is premised solely on peer professional opinion, that is, the Bolam-Bolitho test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is since the principle of patient autonomy has a much smaller role to play in the arena of medical diagnosis and treatment, both of which remain largely within the domains of doctors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new test also prescribes the standard by which the peer professional opinion must assess the information given by healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If Members can look at section 37(2), the first limb is set out in (2)(a)(i).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the second limb, in section 37(2)(a)(ii), the healthcare professional must give his patient information that he knows or ought reasonably to know is material to that “specific” patient for the purpose of making the same informed decision as in the first limb.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, section 37(2)(a)(i) provides for what you might do for a typical patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is judged by what the peers would regard as appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The second limb requires the professional to also think about what might be material to this patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Material information falls into either of two categories, which are set out in section 37(3).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, if it relates to specific concerns or queries that the patient expressly communicates in relation to undergoing the treatment or on the medical advice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, an express question or query or some discussion raised by the patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If a doctor is asked a specific question, that becomes something he has to explain.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, in the second limb in section 37(3)(b), where it relates to specific concerns or queries which the patient does not expressly communicate, but which ought to be apparent from the medical records of the patient which the healthcare professional has reasonable access to and ought reasonably to review.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a bit of a mouthful, but let me explain why it is couched this way and to ensure that Members in this House understand it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the avoidance of doubt, any concerns expressly communicated by a patient have to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The work group was quite unanimous in the view that if it has been brought up expressly to the doctor, then the doctor has to address those queries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In short, in that scenario, the patient can be assured that when he walks into a clinic and sees a doctor, there really are no “stupid questions”.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Every question that this patient raises with this doctor, is a valid, relevant question that has to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is not the intention and clearly, that is not also provided for in the statute.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is also not practical or feasible in practice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What is reasonable is a matter to be assessed in the context of each case and it is not possible to define upfront, at the start, all the categories, in a closed fashion, of information that will be regarded as reasonable or not reasonable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, therefore, the older the medical records are, the less likely it would be that it would be reasonable to expect the healthcare professional to review them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But if there is an old medical record or an old investigation that is labelled, and you put a bright sticky tape on it and it is taped to the front of the file in an obvious way, and it makes some notes about this person's history from some years ago – perhaps an unusual investigation that has taken place or perhaps an allergy that would not be easily discerned from trawling through the files – then it would make it harder for that healthcare professional to say that that is something that he ought not look at in the context of this treatment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Other relevant factors to the assessment would include what transpired during the discussion that the patient has had with the doctor and how the query or concern was characterised in the previous medical records.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if something is mentioned in passing and does not feature prominently across the spectrum of the medical records, then it is less likely that it would be something that ought to be apparent to the doctor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To enhance the understanding of how the provision operates, the Bill provides an illustration at section 37(3)(b) on when information that is not expressly communicated to the attending doctor will be considered material.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The illustration of a patient undergoing a total knee reconstruction in that case is by no means intended to define or circumscribe what is “reasonable” in every case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is just intended to give an example of what could or would satisfy the requirements of reasonableness in the illustration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The third limb, by contrast, addresses the other side of the equation; it asks whether there is reasonable justification on the part of the healthcare professional in situations where information is not given.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill contains several illustrations in this regard.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, there may be reasonable justification for not providing information in a situation of emergency or where a patient has waived his right of information by telling the healthcare professional that he does not want to be given information, and that can be established.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whether there is a waiver is a matter of fact – sometimes of mixed fact and law – and the peer professional opinion can assist in the forensic analysis and weighing up of whether there has been such a waiver by the Judge or tribunal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, you cannot make up your mind for the patient and then, decide, based on that end outcome, what information you will or will not tell the patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If Members can look at section 37(4), this recognises that there may be diversity of views amongst healthcare professionals, all of which are in-principle equally valid for consideration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But, of course, for each of them to be logical, they have to cohere with the standards and pass the test of logic and reasonableness, in the manner which I have described earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Section 37(6) of the Bill provides that the test applies not only in respect of medical advice given to patients, but also medical advice given to a person who is responsible for making a decision about undergoing a treatment or following a particular piece of medical advice on behalf of someone else – that someone else being a patient who is otherwise, legally disabled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A legally disabled person is someone who does not have the mental competence to make the decision for himself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, a parent would be responsible for making a decision on behalf of his infant child.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is defined in section 37(7) of the Bill to mean an individual practicing a profession that provides medical advice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This includes doctors, dentists and oral health therapists, and is not an exhaustive list.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The scope is broad enough to include any individual who practices a profession that provides medical advice, or for which it can be shown that there exists peer professional opinion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We appreciate, Sir, that, beyond the language and contours of the legislation itself, healthcare professionals will require detailed guidance on what is required from them under the new test in practice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We fully agree and we intend to provide such guidance, working with the professional bodies, also the SMC and the CMEP to do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That in fact, was something that the work group itself had proposed as a draft in its report and we will use that as a basis to start the revision of the ethical code and guidelines.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There was in fact, a strong recommendation by the work group to do so to reduce the ECEG into basic core irreducible principles of professional conduct, and use that to gauge and guide doctors in terms of where that bright white line ought to be when it comes to the thresholds.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We believe it endows it with more clarity and certainty.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Healthcare professionals will also have the assurance that they will be evaluated on the basis of a peer who can assess and also contextualise the standard required to that of a clinical setting, which is important because as I have said, no two patients and no two consultations are identical.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, it maintains the high degree of patient autonomy that was present in the Hii Chii Kok test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we strive to move away from a test that is described as patient-centric or a doctor-centric, but instead to one where we can say that it is really undergirded by patient empowerment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Patient autonomy and certainty in the medico-legal climate for doctors cannot be mutually exclusive ideals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They can exist in a virtuous cycle and in the process, build more trust into the patient-doctor relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that ultimately, is the overriding objective of designing this test and adopting it in a way in which I have just outlined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Broadly, these amendments seek to strengthen the system, make it more robust, and deal with as many of the problems that have been identified in the cases that I have outlined and also beyond that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is the second slate of amendments that we are proposing, arising out also of the work group's recommendations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both doctors and the public alike must trust in this outcome, know that it will be independent and transparent and also be able to enforce standards that are fair and consistent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If this system falls short, it undermines confidence and in turn, will affect doctors’ practices and erode trust, in the way I have outlined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments in this Bill are quite substantial and I do not propose to cover every clause, probably to your relief, Sir.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I would add, Sir, that it is not a silver bullet.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You cannot look at the provisions in and of itself, and so, we would like Members to look at these amendments as a collective whole.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because you cannot just change the process or you cannot just impose a time discipline or you cannot just say enhance training.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have got to be all taken into account together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments that we seek to introduce broadly strive towards four objectives, which I will organise my speech around and then highlight the salient clauses in relation to each of these objectives to Members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When the disciplinary system does not effectively enforce the profession's standards, doctors are faced with uncertainty and unnecessary stress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In these cases, the patient-doctor relationship is sometimes supplanted by the plaintiff-doctor relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We seek to introduce a number of changes to enhance the structure and to give more robustness to the disciplinary framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will be a body that is separate from the SMC, headed by a senior doctor as President.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is envisaged that the President will be a full-time appointment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The DC will have a dedicated secretariat that will exclusively support its functions and it will have two key mandates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will be responsible for constituting the DTs in each of the cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will set up the DTs and ensure the personnel is appropriate for the DTs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is in place of the current SMC, which through its secretariat, assists in setting up the DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This addresses concerns about the independence of the DTs from the SMC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, the DT is independent of the SMC which also acts on behalf of the complainant as the prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, there is a continuing perception of the lack of independence simply because the SMC appoints the DT and also has a prosecution arm looking after the complaints of the complainant and framing the charges against the doctor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is ostensibly because as I said, they appoint the DT, but the reality is that it is not suggested that the DT is influenced in any way by the SMC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But nonetheless, this perception is a troubling one, with the potential to undermine confidence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want the impartiality to be not just real but to be seen, to be obviously separate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are not starting from a clean slate as it were in this case as we looked at their practices in other countries, other jurisdictions, and the one that is fairly close to what we are proposing is found in the United Kingdom.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the DC, it will be responsible for the setting up of the DTs to hear the cases as tribunal and the SMC will continue with the function of preferring the charges and prosecuting the charges on behalf of the complainants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The DC’s second key mandate is to oversee the training of members of the Complaints Panel and the Health Committee, and ensure that they are appropriately trained to carry out their roles in the various committees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This addresses various feedback both from members of the CCs and DTs and also from doctors in the town halls that we need to increase and uphold the standards of doctors who sit in these tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many of them are experienced doctors, but sometimes marrying the experience as doctors to a process that has a fairly strong legal slant to it may not always make for a good match.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Other than providing for this, training, regular and systemic training will also help them to carry out their duties better.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is something that the DC will oversee to ensure that the various disciplinary committees are staffed by well-trained, up-to-date and competent members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As a step to ensuring consistency in processes and outcomes, we are proposing that a legal professional is required to sit on each DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Previously, DTs were constituted in various permutations, and it was not obligatory to have a legal professional sit in one of these tribunals, but our view is that having an experienced legal professional on the DT will bring greater legal and forensic expertise to the DTs' deliberations and determinations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, the quasi-judicial nature of DT hearings means that they also invariably require the consideration and application of legal concepts and forensic analysis, such as the application of the standard of proof and assessing the weight and relevance of evidence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In some of the more difficult cases, the key issues may also be more legal rather than medical in nature.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, having a legally trained member sit on the DT will assist the DT in preparing his decisions, ensuring that they are legally sound and structured and also ensure that there is a consistent body of decisions to guide future DTs in their decision making.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In some cases where the DC President might regard as being more complex or novel or perhaps raise novel issues of law, they may be more appropriately directed to a serving Judge or Judicial Commissioner of the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there is an opening or option in section 59 for the President of the DC to decide on a case being more complex and inviting the Chief Justice to nominate a Judge or a JC to sit as a Chairman of that particular DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The legal professional will not necessarily be the chairman of the DT and further, a serving Judge or JC will only chair cases where the President of the DC feels that it is appropriate to do so, and the decisions of the DT will still be determined by majority vote.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Even in a case where a Judge or JC sits as a Chairman, that person cannot on his or her own override the opinion of two doctors if both doctors agree with each other.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The committee has completed its work and the SMC published these guidelines in July 2020.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These will complement the current amendments to facilitate fair, consistent decision making by the DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The next change we are proposing is to introduce greater legal support throughout the system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is to strive to improve the quality of decision making at every level of the process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The advisory arm of this unit will advise the disciplinary committees in their disciplinary framework and ensure that they have access to legal support that they require to perform the functions, and this in turns facilitates clarity on the applicable standards, how the charges might be preferred, what kind of legal standards will apply and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The prosecution arm of the new unit will undertake prosecutions for the SMC; a topic that I will return to later.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While the creation of the new Legal Advisory and Prosecution Unit does not in itself require legislative amendment and will be effected by the SMC administratively, I thought to highlight this to Members as they reflect an important part of the structural changes being made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So later on, when I deal with the IC and the RC, Members should also recall that the legal unit does sit and is present to assist the IC at the outset.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The moment a case is referred to the IC, the IC gets legal support to assess the case, to assess whether it is vexatious or frivolous and whether or not it meets the required threshold for professional misconduct.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next Sir, the amendment will also provide that it is the SMC rather than the CC which will determine whether a matter is referred to the DT or not.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, the MRA requires the SMC to appoint a DT if the CC determines that a formal inquiry by the DT is necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, a typical CC will be appointed; it will be a three member CC and if the CC, after deciding that it needs to be sent to the DT, currently the SMC has got no role to play in that process and the matter goes to the DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is the case even if the SMC might otherwise disagree with the view of the CC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: During the work group's consultations, both the SMC as well as the medical community felt that the SMC should play a more proactive role in ensuring that it is aware of the outcomes of complaints and that there is also a more consistent and uniform filter that the SMC can play before it goes to the DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The medical community feels that the SMC as a whole, has to take ownership and oversight of handling of complaints and not just delegate this to a CC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we believe that the collective wisdom of the SMC in reviewing the CC's decision will also act as a check to ensure that the threshold for professional misconduct is met or at least met in a prima facie way before the matter is referred to the DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If a CC recommends a formal inquiry by the DT, it will also have to formulate the charges and give its reasons for recommending the referral of the complaint to a DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At present, the moment the CC recommends that the matter should be heard by the DT, it finishes its functions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It passes the matter on and then a new team, almost, takes over.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Here, once the CC has decided, it states its reasons and it will also at least formulate the charges, if not fully, as least in draft, so that the DT or the prosecution at that stage, will know the thinking of the CC and know what were the considerations by the CC in referring the matter to the DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the other hand, if the SMC determines after the recommendation by the CC, that the case should not proceed to a formal inquiry then under section 46(7), it must inform the parties of its determination and the reasons for this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the fact that it has decided not to take up the CC's recommendation and also its reasons for not doing so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It may also take a range of alternative actions such as issuing letters of advice, or warning; or perhaps directing the doctor to seek and undergo medical or psychiatric treatment or counselling in the appropriate cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is also in line with what is currently the system with the Law Society, a similar system where the Council of the Law Society makes the final decision on whether to take further action in relation to a complaint after it receives the recommendations from the Inquiry Committee or IC in this case, which is the Law Society's equivalent of the CC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Section 46(2) provides that it must be a case where there is a cause of sufficient gravity for formal inquiry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We wanted to do this to ensure that there is at least a gate or a threshold before the matter is referred to the DT and the relevant members of both the CC and the SMC apply their minds to the standards that have to be established.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I do not need to repeat that here, but those will be the criteria and we would require the SMC members to have regard to that pronouncement in making the assessment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amendments to provide for the SMC to determine if a DT to be appointed as well as prescribing the standards for referral, overall, we believe would allow for greater consistency of cases and also an overall uniformity of standards to be applied.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So that as far as possible, whilst I have said, no two cases are alike, but the gravamen between the cases should result in a similar outcome in terms of the disciplinary process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these issues do arise and what we have done is to look at some very specific measures to ensure that it is more expeditious.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Overall, Members will know from the Bill that there is an overarching timeline that applies to the conduct of the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am not going to go into the specific timelines, but at each stage there is a timeline, there is some provision for extensions beyond certain number of extensions, the relevant committees will have to go to the High Court to make a case for that extension.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we believe that that is the really the best way of driving this forward in a fair way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But of course, in the cases, which are more complex, require more time and more investigations, parties can apply to Court and justify that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will just quickly outline the measures that we have set up in the Bill to address the delays.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are first, an early notification to a doctor that a complaint has been filed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, part of the problem is the doctors do not always know immediately and sometimes it takes months, if not a year, before the doctor is aware that a complaint has been made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, we strive to increase the pool of Complaints Panel members because the Complaints Panel really is the bottleneck.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the Complaints Panel is more well resourced, better staffed, then these cases can proceed more expeditiously and they enable disciplinary committees to be constituted more quickly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, introducing a time limit – time limitation period for complaints.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is also similar to what is done in the Law Society to ensure that very stale complains do not get refreshed, really to ensure that there is also fairness in terms of having the doctors maintain his or her notes and the evidence and the quality of the evidence does not diminish if the complaint is an old one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are provisions for exceptions to be made in cases where patients are unable to or did not know they can still seek leave, justify that and complaints can still be brought despite the time bar.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Fourth, we have created, as I mentioned just now, levers to control both individual stages of the proceedings as well as the overall length of time that the complaint takes to be resolved.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are just two areas which are relatively new and I just want to spend a bit more time on them, to explain this to Members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have proposed a new filter mechanism up front, to help to sieve out unmeritorious complaints at an early stage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To give Members some idea of the thinking behind this, I will just give you some of the numbers that we have.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Quite a significant percentage of these complaints are eventually found to be of no merit, either because they did not pass muster in terms of the standards; or the facts were found to be of a different sort than what was advanced by the patient; or it was otherwise vexatious in a sense that it was a repeat complaint; or a complaint that has been dredged up when it has already been resolved and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is a fair number of cases that do not end up in the DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The thinking behind having the IC is to have more resources upfront to evaluate these cases better, early, and direct more attention to them and dispose of them where possible upfront.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because as one can imagine, if you have the full 165 cases travel through the system, it will create a lot more strain on the resources and it will take a lot more time for each of the cases to be resolved.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, having more specialised and dedicated resources upfront, will play in our view, a significant role in filtering out the cases appropriate either for resolution, early resolution, or perhaps channelling into mediation and then only allowing those that require investigation or have merit in the substance of the complaint to proceed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This rule is not designed to shut them out because we do know, on one hand, that making a complaint is a serious matter and complainants are expected to substantiate the allegations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, complaints will not be dismissed out of head simply because they do not have the requisite level of information or the level of detail that is needed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the appropriate cases, the IC will also direct that this will be either investigated further, or for the complaints committee to take it up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In any event, if the complaint is dismissed, the IC will be required to give its reasons for the decision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is the SMC's practice currently to inform complainants of the outcome of the complaints.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will continue to be the case even after the amendments come into force and the complainants will of course be informed if an IC dismisses their complaint along with the reasons for that dismissal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Once the CC is appointed, it then takes over and assumes oversight of those investigations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Similar to the Review Committee of the Legal Profession Act or LPA, which some Members might be familiar with, there is no right of appeal from the IC's decision to another committee in the disciplinary process or to a Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, this does not preclude judicial review which is present and that is governed by general law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some might think that the CC could play this function and do this filter role.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the reasons I have set out earlier, as to why allowing these cases to be resolved earlier rather than to have them channel through the system, take up committee time, investigation resources, it is for that reason that we propose to have a filter up front and staffed better, more resource and also in tandem with the legal advisory unit that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I just want to also mention to Members that the creation of the IC also parallels the Legal Profession Act which has a similar filtering committee and I think it is called the Review Committee.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me talk about the Review Committee or RC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a new creation; that is why I will spend some time on this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is some feedback that the existing process for appeals was either not transparent or was slow; and sometimes unclear as to what the considerations were; and sometimes new evidence was let in, in those cases which then led to the process being derailed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I hasten to add that this RC is not intended to be a second CC and so the scope will be limited to two specific instances: First, whether or not there has been due process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it looks at the CC and evaluates it from the position of whether due process has been complied with.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, to assess whether any new evidence has been submitted to an RC and if so, why and it will consider whether the new evidence is material to the complaint or to the outcome, as the case may be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, we seek to empower the IC and the CC to obtain relevant documents and information for the purposes of their inquiries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think it can brook no dissent that the relevant investigative arms of this process must be clothed with the power to obtain documents, take information as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the new sections 43(2) and 45(5) provide for that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, we seek to also provide that the investigator can look into wrongdoings not covered by the complaint.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is something that we considered for some time because there are two schools of thought.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One, if it is not contained in the four corners of the complaint, then why should the investigation start to look into this?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, you can investigate it at the same time, file a new complaint and I believe this is an improvement over the current process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, allowing for interim orders to be issued more expediently in appropriate cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It seeks to introduce a framework for the Interim Orders Committee (IOC).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We provided for the IOC to be constituted more expediently and to act more quickly in circumstances where there is an imminent threat to the health or safety of doctors' patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under the current MRA, the referrals to the IOC are made by the Chairman of the Complaints Panel.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The SMC does not have power to refer complaints to the IOC on its own accord and the effect of this is that where the SMC learns of matters which might warrant a referral to the IOC, it is reliant on the Chairman of the Complaints Panel to do so, and we regard this as less than ideal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under the current MRA, the doctor must be heard at an IOC hearing in all cases before the order is made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, with the best of intentions, sometimes, these hearings will take place weeks, if not months, after the referral is first made, for a number of reasons, not necessarily because of an intention to delay.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The new section 59K provides that an IOC can make an interim order immediately, without first giving the doctor the right to be heard in certain exceptional situations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And these situations are limited to two types.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, where a Court of law in Singapore has found that a doctor has engaged in conduct alleged in the complaint or information and the conduct poses an imminent danger to the health or safety of any of the doctor's patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, a finding of this has been made by a Court in Singapore and the SMC is of the view that this doctor's continued practice would pose an imminent danger to his patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, where the SMC is of the opinion that such conduct poses an imminent danger to the health or safety of any of the doctor's patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the thresholds are high, but we regard this as being in the interest of patient safety and public interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In situations where such an interim order is made, the IOC must then convene the hearing within one month where the doctor will then be heard on his position and the interim order can then either be revoked or it can be replaced, as the case may be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the hearing is not able to be convened within the month, then the immediate interim order will lapse.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, this also seeks to preserve the balance between the SMC and the doctor's livelihood.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is to ensure a greater diversity of representation and views.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The SMC is the paramount body that regulates and also represents the medical community, and it is important that its composition reflects the range of views amongst the different groups and also the different range of seniorities in the medical profession.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the amended section 4 makes two key changes to the composition of the SMC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the major medical professional bodies will now be represented on the SMC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, these are the Academy of Medicine Singapore, the College of Family Physicians Singapore and the Singapore Medical Association.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will be represented by their respective Master or Presidents, as the case may be, or by a member of their respective councils, as nominated by the President or the Master.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, there will now be one instead of two representatives from each medical school in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This could be the Dean or his representative.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We hope that this will encourage younger and also more doctors to step forward and serve on the SMC and on the Complaints Panel.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have set out some provisions which allow for this and, in the interest of time, I will not go into that but to ask members to look at section 47 which empowers the IC to refer a complaint to mediation during its inquiry; this section similarly empowers the CC also to do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the parties are participating in the mediation, obviously, if you are in the middle of a mediation, you do not want to have also a disciplinary inquiry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the IC or the CC may, having regard to the progress of the mediation, suspend the inquiry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will work with institutions, like the Singapore Mediation Centre, to provide the relevant expertise and also infrastructural settings to achieve better outcomes through the use of well-trained, highly qualified mediators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There will be a reporting obligation for mediators who will report to the IC and CC to ensure that one keeps an even keel on the progress of the mediation and it is not used as an excuse to dislodge or disrupt the timetable for the conduct of the disciplinary proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When that work group canvassed views, particularly from doctors, there were some who expressed the concern that the use of private law firms for prosecution may sometimes result in a "I must get a conviction at all costs" kind of approach and that is not the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But it is also not healthy that there is that impression.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will aggregate the cases, build up experience to be able to handle prosecutions and to have, residing within the SMC, institutional knowledge and the collective wisdom of what it would take to prosecute these cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, itself, will lend consistency across the spectrum as to how a charge might be framed and the factors to be taken into account in mitigation or aggravation as the case may be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have mentioned to Members, these have all to be taken together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It remains only for me to thank the work group members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also want to record my appreciation to the members of the three professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have been very supportive of our efforts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They also have people sitting on the work group and they have also recorded their agreement and support for the changes reflected in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will speak on the Civil Law (Amendment) Bill and my colleague, Mr Leon Perera, will speak on the amendments to the Medical Registration (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For my speech, I will focus on the promulgation of the standard of care for medical advice in the proposed section 37, which I will refer to as the section 37 test, and the work group report on which the section 37 test is based.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, there are many positives about the Bill and the work group report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, there remains some residual concerns about the section 37 test, which I will go into.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, I will make a point about the importance of an eye needing to be kept on the future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I wish to thank the work group for its fine work and well-written report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have sought feedback from some doctors on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One consistent feedback that was shared almost unanimously was that the feedback from doctors on the systemic issues surrounding both informed consent and the SMC disciplinary process was taken very seriously by the work group and the Ministry respectively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As one doctor put it, and I quote: "The work group report succinctly captures the sentiment of doctors." When I read the feedback given by doctors in the report, it was refreshing to read what came across in an unvarnished yet professional way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the doctors and others who came forward to give feedback are also to be acknowledged and thanked.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some doctors have said that the amendment is well thought out and would be welcomed by the medical community.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would go some way towards mitigating defensive medicine which, as we know, increases healthcare costs without necessarily improving medical outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Overall, the work group report and the section 37 test are significant steps in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The work group itself recommends further steps, including Recommendation 3, the development of nationally agreed speciality specific and situational guidelines to deal with standard commonplace procedures in each speciality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am sure this House and the public look forward to the speedy publication of those guidelines as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first query concerns how the proposed section 37 will be applied in Singapore Medical Council or SMC disciplinary cases going forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Its application to future civil proceedings covering medical negligence is not in doubt.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, in light of the work group report’s recommendations to amend the SMC Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines or ECEG on informed consent, as detailed in Annex F of the work group’s report, how will the proposed section 37 interface with SMC disciplinary proceedings where a doctor is deemed to meet the threshold of the “serious negligence” limb of professional misconduct?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prima facie, it ought to follow that the section 37 test would apply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, and in view of the High Court’s judgment in Lim Lian Arn on the correct understanding of the ECEG with respect to professional misconduct, clarification by the Minister on this point would be helpful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One is the difficulties faced by doctors who have a limited time with patients.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The work group report in Annex C sets out the feedback received from doctors on informed consent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Among other points, doctors gave feedback that, and I quote: “Thorough consent-taking is not possible in every setting, especially in the polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Doctors may be burdened with other onerous administrative duties and have heavy caseloads.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are simply not afforded enough time to build a relationship with the patient.” This feedback was given in relation to the perceived impracticality of satisfying all the requirements of the Modified Montgomery test.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The concern with the section 37 test is that it does not seem to solve this issue raised in the feedback.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the section 37 test still requires the idiosyncrasies of patients to be taken into account, it may still remain very difficult to take consent thoroughly in a polyclinic setting.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In that time, the doctor has to gather the patient's history, examine him or her, discuss treatment options and refer the matter to a specialist or as appropriate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, the doctor has to comply with the section 37 test when it comes into force.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Not only does the doctor have to answer queries from the patient, as provided in sub-section 3(a) which can already take up time, sub-section 3(b) requires that even if the patient does not ask, the doctor must assess whether any information is material to the patient when reviewing the patient's medical records.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And it is unclear from section 37 how far back the doctor should look, after all the records of an elderly patients can go back decades – although I note Minister's point about reasonableness in his Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The only statutory illustration provided for in sub-section 3(b) concerns knee replacement surgery which is a major procedure done by orthopaedic specialists and for which a doctor will certainly have more time for consultation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But based on this sole illustration, a doctor working in a polyclinic and even a general practitioner in private practice may be hard pressed to know what is practically expected of them in dealing with large number of patients with short consultation times.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Increasing the consultation time is not a practical solution because it comes with costs too, in terms of higher waiting times, higher consultation fees in proportion to the times spent and even stress on doctors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another concern that some doctors raised over the section 37 test to me is the difficulties that may arise when multiple doctors are involved in the patient's care, also known as team management, especially in large public hospitals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The patient may have many concerns documented by different doctors of varied specialties over a period of time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If a doctor who finally takes the consent inadvertently does not address one of the possible risks, especially one that is outside his or her speciality, would it be fair to hold this against him or her?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is similar to one of the points raised by doctors to the work group and I quote, "Practitioners face an inordinate number of challenges in getting proper informed consent in team settings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is partly due to restrictions of time, exigencies of service, operational efficiency and the lack of familiarity with patients".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The section 37 test carries potentially serious consequences for doctors who are found not to be in compliance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would not be ideal or helpful if the application of section 37 test raises doubts that can only be properly clarified in test cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because it is not only doctors who will suffer the consequences.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All of us tend to lose if defensive medicine is practised due to uncertainty, whether in terms of over-treatment and the associated higher costs, longer waiting times, higher taxes or poorer healthcare outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More fundamentally, regular reviews would be consistent with the evolution of medical care in Singapore, where individual rights and patient autonomy continue to move centre stage and reflect the current and future realities of medical practice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prospect of the doubling of the elderly population by 2030 and by extension more complicated or multiple medical conditions from a patient requiring overlapping advice and consultation may well be a harbinger for increased misunderstanding between patients and doctors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our multicultural local setting, added complications could arise in view of potential language barriers in some cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, the positives surrounding the work group Report and proposed Bill; second, the residual concerns about the section 37 test; and third, the need to keep an eye on the future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also declare my interest as the son of a cancer patient.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All of us have loved ones who have been through the journey of illness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All of us know of stories, whether family, friends, residents being diagnosed – wondering what the next step is on the treatment journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Grappling with uncertainty – whether from the perspective of a patient, or being the loved one looking on wanting the best for the patient, our loved one.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The intent is to help patients, and to help doctors to help patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But I have questions to ask, both on the detail and on the bigger picture and my questions fall into three sections: the law, the process and the big picture – making patient safety better, helping patients better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On the law, I want to ask about this new statutory test.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I understand the Minister has shared there was consultation with the legal profession.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For the benefit of those of us in this debate who are non lawyers, we will be happy to hear more on what was the legal profession's view.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Minister spoke about engaging patient advocacy groups.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister share in greater detail what patients think of this and whether patients across a broad range of socio-economic backgrounds were engaged as well?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because the informational needs and concerns and worries of the Ah Gong, the Ah Ma living in a 1-room, 2-room HDB flat, are very different from the very well informed professional going to see a doctor.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is something that every practitioner faces every day and having confidence that the Ministry has looked at that is going to be very much part of looking at these reforms.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Minister also said that there were comparable legislative moves in other jurisdictions like Australia.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister confirm that these were recalibrations or codifications of case law?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How does the Ministry foresee Disciplinary Tribunals and the Courts adjudicating on this?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And if a Disciplinary Tribunal or the Courts happens to prefer one particular body or peer opinion, does that shape the weight in which that body will be considered in subsequent Disciplinary Tribunals or Courts' decisions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And if the new structures are to deliver justice and outcomes well for patients and for doctors, there must be adequate resourcing and manpower – whether to support the Inquiry Committee, the revised Complaints Committee or the workings of the SMC.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know that when justice is unduly delayed, it is unfair for the patients and families, who spend years wondering what the outcome will be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Delayed justice is also unjust to an accused who will go for years not knowing if he or she will be found guilty or innocent.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, Mr Speaker, it would also be a disservice to patients and doctors together if strict, speedy timelines are pushed, but without sufficient resources to do the job thoroughly and fairly.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister confirm and assure us that there will be sufficient resourcing and how will the resourcing be budgeted for?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
