text: Allowing a Disciplinary Tribunal to appoint experts is an important reform because we know that in an adversarial system, there is always a risk, whether real, implied or subconscious, that an adversarial spirit will permeate the adversarial proceedings.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Disciplinary Tribunal's own expert witness can thus be a second opinion to each side’s expert opinions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You might say a third opinion or a third way: a moderating force, a stabiliser when there are differences in expert opinion.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Indeed, some jurisdictions have explored having the experts convened together in a less structured way, they call it “hot tubbing”; and these current reforms introduce an aspect of that.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because the first duty of the expert witness is not the side that is hiring them, but to the truth.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, expert witnesses must continue seeking the truth together and not as adversaries.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Beyond the changes to the law and the regulatory framework, we must also look at the bigger picture.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How do we help doctors and healthcare workers to keep patients safe, to provide better care?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is important for Complaints Panels too, which must draw people from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The new section 39 allows a doctor of eight years’ experience to be appointed to the Complaints Panel.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, Sir, what is on paper and the actual extent of representation – the actual extent of representation matters too because when you speak with junior doctors, young doctors out on the ground; busy, running, doing everything they can to keep patients going, to keep patients alive, our junior doctors have that certain closeness to the ground, especially on the inpatient wards.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our junior doctors have that sense of the actual working experience, actual working conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Whether it is implementing the decisions of a senior, more experienced doctor, or caring for patients in the middle of the night on call, a 24-hour shift, 36-hour shift or in the old days – and I am starting to sound like an older doctor – even longer shifts by those seniors who came before some of us.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But these views from the ground from our junior doctors, our younger doctors, they add important colour to the understanding of healthcare delivery every day on the ground.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And on the ground, especially in healthcare, implementation is reality.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Indeed, Sir, over the years, in some hospitals, it is our younger doctors – working together with nurses, allied health, medical social workers, healthcare administrators, mentors – who help bring change and transformation, keeping open eyes, open minds and open hearts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Seeing through the eyes of patients to make the journey safer and better for all.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Seeing through the eyes of healthcare workers so that our people can do their best – and do even better – to look after patients, keep patients safer, lower the risk of human error.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because when a human error happens, it is not always just about one human.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to mention a case reported in the media.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In referring to this case, I take reference from public domain media reports, in particular, a Straits Times article from 18 January 2006.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Staff nurse Mdm Leong was the only one at the home who knew of the drug allergy but she omitted to inform the doctor who was going to see the patient at a subsequent hospital appointment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This drug was later given to the patient who had an allergy to it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, you might say the coroner was bound legally to find that there was neglience.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But the coroner also noted the challenging circumstances she worked under.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How can you expect a nurse who has to take care of all 180 residents to also provide the standard of care that is expected to be given to sick patients?" Sir, I still remember how troubled I was to read about what happened because as healthcare workers, we are all in this together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When a fellow doctor does not deliver that care to the patient, we feel for the patient and we ask, "How can we help that doctor to do better?" When a nurse has been put in a difficult situation and things have not gone well, we believe in standing by our fellow healthcare workers as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In a letter to the Straits Times that year in 2006, I wrote, "It is true that nurses – while human and thus fallible – owe a duty of care to their patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yet care is not provided by individuals alone, but by organisations and the systems set up therein.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When accidents occur, it is crucial to look not just at the individuals involved in making the error but also the system and organisation." Nurses, doctors, healthcare workers – like everyone in this House, human and thus fallible.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we know healthcare is not provided by individuals alone but by organisations and systems.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The airplane pilot has ultimate responsibility for operation and safety in-flight.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But safety goes beyond the pilot and the airline industry recognises this deep truth.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The International Civil Aviation Organization's or ICAO Safety Management Manual looks at the relationship between humans and workplace.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They call it the "SHELL" model – software, hardware, environment and liveware.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Software – the procedures, training and support; hardware – the machines and equipment; environment – the workplace in which everything and everyone functions; and liveware – humans, people who have to work with software, hardware and the working environment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, it is critical that MOH continues to touch the ground and look at systems factors as part of root cause analysis when mishaps occur.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because nobody starts their day thinking of doing harm.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: No medical professional, no healthcare worker, no nurse starts their day intending to cause harm.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to continue making workplaces safer and reducing the risk of human error.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have to keep on improving because the day a belief sets in that improvement is not possible or not worth striving for, that is the day our system will ossify and begin to decay.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must stand against the belief that improvement is not possible.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have today discussed the duty to advise as part of informed consent.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In Question Time earlier, I spoke about seeking truth from data, seeking truth from facts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How does this time compare with the average time slot provided for a patient consultation?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How often do healthcare workers have to go the extra mile by finding time and doing these communications outside of official clinic working hours?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But our healthcare institutions, processes and management have a critical role too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I stand in support of these two Bills.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before proceeding, I would like to refer to the revelation of my hon friend, Dr Tan Wu Meng, informing that his father is a cancer patient.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The key question is this: what is good advice from a doctor that is in keeping with the trust that the patient reposes in his or her doctor?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is advice that cannot be faulted by a patient for being incomplete, medically unsound or in any way that does not respect his autonomy and ability to make decisions for his own health.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A patient decides based on two things – first, what he knows and second, what he thinks the doctor is telling him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first is a function of metaphysics – what he feels he wants in life, his current state, his tolerance for uncertainty, suffering or more prosaic things such as personal finances, what he wants to leave behind, what he wants to use up in this life and his relationship with his family.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And it is this second part which I would like to speak on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have two specific points to make: first, let us be clear on what balance we wish to strike between the recognition of medical expertise and patient autonomy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not find it useful to call the first "paternalistic" and the second "patient-centric" because of the negative overtones in the first and for the positive in the second.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I make this clarification at the start because there is some risk of doublespeak if we were to use these words without care as to their meaning.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Take for example the report from the work group to review the taking of informed consent and SMC disciplinary processes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister referred to the stupendous work that this work group did and I join him in the laudatory remarks that he made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not say whether this is right or wrong but merely to point out where the needle is moving – and we ought not try and give it a veneer of political correctness by calling it "patient-centric".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A model that focuses on the patient means we regard the materiality and relevance of information from the perspective of the patient.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The new test measures this by reference to opinion of a responsible body of doctors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some critics may argue that this new test will in fact emasculate the "patient-centric" element.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the first point on which I seek clarification.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, in relation to disclosure of information that a healthcare professional knows or ought reasonably to know, the legal standard of care is measured from the perspective of a reasonable patient in the patient's situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is not an end by itself but to facilitate the patient to make an informed decision on the advice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The work group in its report refers to confusion and anxiety amongst many doctors arising from the application of the "reasonable patient" standard who believe that this will give rise to defensive medicine and more litigation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister, made a similar comment today as well and he referred to this as more of perceived uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I fully agree with the honourable Minister with his views.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, if that is the case, perhaps we could deal directly with the perception of the doctors instead of introducing a new standard of care.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, would it not be the case if a patient who is provided advice that is based on the standard of care requiring him to reasonably understand and expect it, that there should be a lesser chance of him suing his doctor?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that the Bill itself does not make the claim of being "patient-centric".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, I recognise the role of professional expertise in any decision-making.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Being a professional myself, I hope my clients concede that I do know the law in a manner that they do not.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What I am asking for is a clear-eyed recognition of the limits of the role of the patient, the role of the doctor and the role of the Court in the finding of fact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, whether a patient has indeed given a waiver to know information relating to a certain decision – that is, when a patient has decided not to decide.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are findings of fact and a place should be reserved for the Court to determine this matter rather than relying on the professional opinion of doctors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As the Minister is aware, the evolution of peer professional advice standard in case law was due to the recognition that in the medical field, it may be impossible to identify a single professional consensus on a specific course of action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, so long as it is a view of a group of competent members of a profession, it suffices.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But when it comes to issues of what a reasonable patient has or has not decided, one can presumably arrive at a more specific finding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, I have been speaking on the interests of doctors and those of the patients and speaking of the needle as if more for one is less for the other.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But as the hon Minister said, the interests of both do coincide in very large areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indeed, it is never in the interest of doctors to violate their Hippocratic Oath and harm their patients.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But the relationship between a patient and a doctor is an unequal one – a point made by the hon Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is unequal in terms of expertise, experience and judgement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is why the law regards the doctor as the patient's fiduciary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The doctor, in the giving of advice, must take this asymmetry into account.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Taken as a whole, the Bill represents an important step in the right direction and I do not oppose the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, there are gaps and issues on which I shall speak to suggest further areas for review and Improvement going forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A furore on the medical community over the taking of informed consent emerged in early 2019 over the case of SMC vs Dr Lim Lian Arn.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: During the COS debates in 2019, I spoke about some of the issues raised by this and other recent cases in respect of the clarity around rules on consent taking and procedural issues with the SMC's disciplinary process, including the rules governing the composition of the SMC itself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This addresses the unsatisfactory situation of complaints being deliberated for years while during that time, a cloud hangs over the head of the medical practitioner who is the complainant.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, it provides for clear separation or clearer separation between the investigation and adjudication arms with the establishment of a new Disciplinary Commission or DC.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Taking a step back and looking at the bigger picture, these clarifications would tend to advance confidence and certainty amongst medical practitioners which may lessen any drift towards defensive medicine.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I will speak about potential gaps and issues in the Bills as it stands and make a number of suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I begin, I declare my interest as the CEO of a research consultancy that there is some work in the healthcare services space.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While some have seen these amendments as lending greater weight in the disciplinary process towards doctors and away from lawyers and while, if true, that would have its merits, as the process would be more akin to discipline being meted out by a jury of one's peers, I wonder if there should be a role for patient advocates, so that the outcomes from the disciplinary process may better balance the interests of different stakeholder groups and will be seen to be performing that role.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is not an idea that is without precedent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency, for example, overseas a regulatory regime which includes performance and professional standards panels that consists of at least three members selected from a list of people approved by the national board.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The panel will include at least half but no more than two-thirds of registered practitioners in the same profession as the practitioners subject to the panel, and at least one person representing the community.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Another interesting example to cite in this regard is Singapore's disciplinary process for accountants.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Public Accountants Oversight Committee or PAOC, operating under ACRA, is authorised to oversee all matters related to the registration of public accountants in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To ensure independence, a majority of PAOC members are not public accountants.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They comprise experienced professionals from the Public Service, the business community and the audit profession.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Providing some degree of representation to patient advocacy groups on such DCs while medical practitioners remain in the majority may be worth considering.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also suggest that legislation consider requiring that a public interest goal that encompasses a recognition of the need to balance all stakeholder interests, including those of patients, non-doctor medical staff and taxpayers be included in the mission statement of the SMC.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: After all, the SMA already exists as something akin to a union for medical practitioners and the SMC should be seen to reflect the broader interests and the greater good.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the same vein, I would also like to ask: the 2019 work group report, which provided the critical inputs for these amendments, largely drew on feedback from doctors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The report did mention that the work group spoke to patient advocacy groups, but did not specify which ones.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, I would like to ask if there will be a requirement for a minimum number of medical practitioners sitting on DCs from the same discipline as that of the medical practitioner who is the subject of a complaint or investigation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would seem sensible, so as to inject relevant clinical expertise into the deliberative process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Doctors come from an array of specialties and backgrounds and may not fully understand the intricacies of cases across the profession.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In Australia, for performance assessments, the national board selects an assessor whose scope of practice is similar to that of the practitioner being assessed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, a general practitioner who works in a rural and remote area might be assessed by a practitioner who is familiar with the particular challenges of rural practice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, in health and performance panels, at least one member must be a registered practitioner in the relevant or same health profession as the practitioners subject to the panel.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The President of the Disciplinary Commission will then decide if it is still "in the public interest" to pursue the case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is possible that the threshold is set very low, in which case, many late cases will be pursued contrary to the reasonableness of the statute of limitations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can the legislation or subsidiary legislation be more specific in describing the scenarios in which it would be permissible for a late complaint to be investigated?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I raise the issue of ensuring sufficient training to members of the these DCs, in a way that is comprehensive and demonstrably.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Judges claimed that if the Complaints Committee members and the Disciplinary Tribunal members as well as both Prosecuting and Defence Counsel had all studied the ECEG properly as well as previous Court of Three Judges' judgments that were relevant, the unjust outcomes could have been avoided.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Beyond the medical aspects of the case, the members may not be familiar with legal concepts, such as rules of natural justice and due process, burden of proof, a minimum standard for professional misconduct, which is an issue of mixed fact and law and proportionate sentencing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in the Soo Shuenn Chiang's case, the DT wrongly accepted the guilty plea because of the failure to properly assess the facts of the case and whether the acts which Dr Soo admitted to, rose to the level of professional misconduct in the first place.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Training of all members involved in the disciplinary process is key to ensuring justice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Section 57(2b) states that the Disciplinary Commission or DC is responsible for training members of the complaints panel or health committee.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For greater rigour, the amendments should include a requirement for certified training in the ECEG and medical law before someone can act in the disciplinary process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such training would surely help raise confidence in the disciplinary processes among the medical community.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I note that the 2019 work group report had recommended that such specialist training in legal matters be provided to members and that the DC should consider working together with the Singapore Judicial College, the Singapore Academy of Law and Singapore Medical Association on the provision of training.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that there are existing training courses provided for being an expert witness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But my suggestion here is for more comprehensive training to all relevant personnel with clear certifiable outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I understand that Minister Edwin Tong did allude to the responsibility of the DC in ensuring that training is provided to DC members and would be grateful for more details on how this will be executed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, the Bill seems to be silent on the question of who the SMC uses as its Prosecuting Counsel.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The current practice of using commercial law firms may be unsustainable due to skyrocketing legal costs, sometimes, at the expense of fair judgments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I did note that, in his Second Reading speech, Minister Edwin Tong did allude to the creation of a legal unit within the SMC as part of the changes that will happen after the passage of this Bill if it is passed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would be curious to know whether all legal work would be handled by this in-house legal unit and there would be no more reliance on outsourced lawyers, or would that be a hybrid model going forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The context for raising this question is as follows.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Legal costs borne by the SMC have been known to be high, potentially posing a concern.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This may result in doctors having to pay more in terms of their contribution to the SMC and medical indemnity insurance, in turn leading to rising healthcare costs borne by consumers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This suggestion would also solve the issue of insufficient legal support provided to the CCs at present.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Members of the legal and prosecution units may be drawn from the Attorney-General's Chambers or from the pool of Legal Services Officers to tap on their legal and prosecutorial experience.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, it is unclear if having in-house counsel would help to save on legal costs compared to outsourcing, that begs the question of whether the SMC has done a cost-benefit analysis of having an in-house legal unit versus continued reliance on outsourcing to commercial law firms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would urge the Government to work with the SMC to look into this question and act accordingly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to raise the possibility of creating a parallel disciplinary process that departs from an adversarial system to an inquisitorial system so that witnesses, that are agreed to by both sides, may be questioned by the DT to form an opinion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Currently, the DT members may sit quietly for much of the proceedings while lawyers and witnesses duel in front of them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An inquisitorial system would remove the incentives and therefore the biases inherent in a "conviction at all costs" attitude on the part of the prosecution.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, an inquisitorial system for the SMC would give more power to the DT in directing the proceedings and offers the advantage of seeking the truth instead of taking sides.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But the adversarial approach is perhaps most appropriate where the defendant needs to prove innocence in relation to a very serious charge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, this point of feedback was raised during a review in 2014.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For this to work, the DT members would need to be adequately trained, as alluded to earlier in my speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to speak on recognition and support for doctors serving in disciplinary committees or as expert witnesses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As a result, active private doctors who run busy practices often decline the invitation to be in the DT.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Yet, it is important to have full-time working doctors in DTs as it ensures its decisions are relevant, up-to-date and reflect ground realities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One point I would make here in passing is that I suggest that the Government and the SMC analyse the current doctor composition on such committees to assess if senior and retired doctors are over-represented.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One doctor in private practice I spoke to, had describe being in the SMC or serving in DTs as a "thankless job".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Another doctor commented that a friend recently mentioned that you received 11-feet high stacks of notes to go through before a case, with little compensation and support to speak of.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The stipend paid to doctors for their service could be increased, but there are of course limits to this as this may tend to raise the fees doctors need to pay for the SMC's costs which may pass through to consumers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One possibility is to automatically assign credit when doctors serve on disciplinary tribunals to count towards doctors' mandatory Continuing Medical Education or CME requirements to maintain good standing as medical practitioners.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, this would need further and consultation so as to be done in a manner that does not compromise CME goals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To meet these new stricter timelines, more resources would need to be made available.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to ask if plans are being made for the SMC to handle the current backlog of cases to be in line with these new requirements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Last but not least, I would like to raise the issue of the composition of the SMC returning to a subject I raised during the 2019 Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Currently, the Government appoints a large number of SMC members.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And in the past the majority of SMC members were not directly elected by the medical practitioner community.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, it would appear that a perception still exists among the medical practitioner community that the SMC acts like a Government arm and as such the outcomes of disciplinary processes may reflect the Government's stance more than what is fair and agreeable to doctors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The counter argument to that kind of perception is that an SMC, where the majority of members are elected from the medical profession, may become a body that tilts more towards the interests of doctors than patients or the wider society, in lieu of the hand of the Government to inject considerations of broader societal interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In considering this question and it is a big question, I would like to suggest that the Government considers regularly measuring the state of opinion among doctors towards the SMC to ensure that confidence is high.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And in light of these findings, consider how best to tweak the balance between elected and appointed seats on the SMC, if at all.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: After all, an SMC which enjoys a high degree of confidence from the medical practitioner community would be a strong bulwark against any creep towards defensive medicine.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is important that patients can trust their doctors and know that their complaints against errant doctors can be heard fairly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Last night, one of my residents, Mr Chua came to see me about his mother, who passed away after taking a straightforward liver test in the hospital.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: His mother was hospitalised for a skin condition.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is in this context that I hope that the debate on the two amendment Bills today, would build trust between patients and doctors, and not less.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I know that it is equally important that doctors need to know of the practical, clear and consistent guidelines to inform their patients on treatment risks so that they can fully serve their patients without fear that patients will end up suing them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But this trust had been under "serious threat of erosion", according to a special work group which was formed in March 2019 to look into this.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The report pointed out that controversial, high-profile cases of medical malpractice which seemed to go on for a long time with outcomes the doctors did not expect, had perhaps made doctors fearful and wonder, "How can I care for my patient without getting into legal trouble?" The work group to review the taking of informed consent and SMC Disciplinary Process has put in a lot of effort into this report, engaging over 1,000 doctors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Arising from their recommendations, which were released in November 2019, we are now at the stage of legalising some of these recommendations through the amendments of the Medical Registration Act or MRA and the Civil Law Act.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: These recommendations will hopefully go a long way in restoring trust.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In a nutshell, the MRA amendments put more responsibility on the medical community to self-regulate, with the creation of new legal advisory unit, dedicated secretariat and new committees.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, many people not in the medical fraternity feedbacked that the Singapore Medical Council or SMC is taking too long to handle and investigate complaints against the doctors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For instance, a doctor's interview in a news report last year, said it took two and a half years for SMC to resolve what she termed as a "frivolous" complaint against her.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, we hope that the legal mechanisms will be able to speed up the process for resolving medical complaints.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I spoke to several doctors and they are general pleased with the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In particular, some senior doctors are glad that the avenue to appeal to the Minister is replaced by a Review Committee which would also include a lay person.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In the light of the new Review Committee, I would like to ask the Minister what will be the selection criteria of the lay person stated in section 2 of Medical Registration (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In most people's mind, we hope that these laymen should be experienced professionals who are older, as they are more likely to have the experience to avoid making radical judgements.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, in tipping the balance toward doctors, I am concerned that this might disadvantage patients in some way, especially those who are lack of resources.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, it is timely to amend the Medical Registration Act to allow the SMC to set up a new Inquiry Committee to improve the efficiency of handling complaints.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If the complaint merits empathy and is not complicated, it will be recommended that the dispute be resolved through mediation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Cases that merits further investigation will be referred to the Complaints Committee.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In general, Singaporeans are not very familiar with medical knowledge.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If patients suspect that they have been misdiagnosed or given the wrong medicine, they often feel that there is no way to lodge a complaint.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I hope Minister can provide help to complainants in 3 areas.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: First, if the complainant feels that the Inquiry Committee is too hasty in dismissing the complaint, can he appeal to MOH?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Second, when the complainant is ordered to go through mediation, can he apply for third-party assistance if necessary?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Third, if the complainant does not have the means to hire a lawyer when he needs to go to court or when he is sued for defamation by the doctor, can he apply for pro-bono legal services?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Overall, we do not want an honest complainant to be denied access to appeals because of a lack of resources.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, the Civil Law and the Medical Registration (Amendment) Bills have given the doctors a better peace of mind and have also benefited the patients.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Through the amendment Bills, SMC has created new legal entities, dedicated secretariat and a few more "C"s such as Inquiry Committee or IC, Disciplinary Commission or DC, Health Committee or HC, Review Committee or RC, Interim Orders Committee or IOC, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, all these "C"s will lead to a higher "C", that is, higher cost.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I will like to ask the Minister who would fund the additional costs?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Do we expect the patients who complain to pay?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Yet, SMC received a grant of almost $1.9 million from MOH in 2019.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Do we expect the taxpayer to pay for the additional costs of the SMC?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I hope the doctors can understand and will not pass this additional fee to their patients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For several doctors, they question whether justice is even on the table and some cases brought by SMC were misguide and ended up being overturned by the High Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Medical Registration (Amendment) Bill is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It helps the process produce fairer, quicker and more consistent outcomes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support the Bill and I would like to thank MOH for convening the work group to review the taking of informed consent and SMC Disciplinary Process in March 2019.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The work group engaged doctors, doctors' associations, patient advocacy groups, lawyers and members of the public, producing a rich report whose imprint is clear in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have some points of clarification on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point relates to manpower, as many have raised before me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill adds several layers to the SMC's disciplinary process to reach its conclusion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By my count, a case may require as many as 17 different committee members not including experts or lawyers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some new measures will help with staffing, such as lifting the limits on the number of non-SMC members who can join the Complaints Panel.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But, I worry that this is not enough, after all, we are talking about a status quo where lack of manpower has delayed the process by years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, of the non-SMC members appointed to the Complaints Panel in 2019, how many were doctors and non doctors?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I ask this because we are lifting the limits on these numbers, but the change will not help if each number is currently nowhere near its limit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, how many Complaints Panel members does the Ministry aim for the Complaints Panel to have in 2021?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What steps will the Ministry take to achieve this target?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point of clarification is on the purpose of the Inquiry Committee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill introduces the idea of the Inquiry Committee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Any time a case reaches the SMC, two doctors from the Inquiry Committee will decide whether the case is frivolous.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If no, they pass it to the Complaints Committee to investigate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have to agree with a group of doctors interviewed by the work group who has said that a new committee is not the solution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The most elegant solution, in my view, is to skip the creation of the Inquiry Committee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We let the Complaints Committee determine whether a case is frivolous but set a deadline of three weeks for them to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the case is not frivolous, they seamlessly continue their investigation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This way, we keep the committee sensitive to time and focused on tasks while avoiding the work of forming new committees and the friction of transferring investigations between them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we do decide to keep the Inquiry Committee, I have two questions for the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What will be done to ensure Inquiry Committees avoid this same exact practice?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point of clarification relates to the dismissal of frivolous, vexatious, misconceived or non substantive complaints by the Inquiry Committee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Minister had earlier addressed this point substantively and I just wanted to confirm that the Inquiry Committee will share its decisions and reasons with the complainant when it dismisses the complaint.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My next point was addressed by the Minister about the legal advisory unit and I will move on to my fifth point, which is about the avenues now available to the medical council in serious cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It can do this when it determines that the order would protect members of the public or otherwise serve the public interest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, when is it appropriate for the medical council to choose not to escalate matters to the Disciplinary Commission?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The existence of discretion suggests that it is sometimes acceptable to the medical council to avoid escalating the matter even when a doctor has caused the death of a patient or has been convicted of a serious criminal offense.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What factors mitigate against the severity of such incidents?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, what are the envisaged cases where an interim order is required and it is deemed "necessary for the protection of members of the public or otherwise in the public's interest"?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What factors or principles should guide the consideration of the Interim Orders Committee?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Three, when should the medical council escalate matters to the Disciplinary Commission as opposed to seeking interim orders?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If a patient's health is being threatened, these two avenues are available to the medical council.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry provide examples where it would be more appropriate to pursue an escalation to the Disciplinary Commission as opposed to seeking interim orders?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I also thank the Ministry for the direction taken in the Civil Law (Amendment) Bill towards a more patient-centric approach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is consistent with the growing international consensus on the need for greater patient autonomy and informed consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My only concern on this Bill is again on manpower and time constraints doctors face.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that doctors have significant concerns on how to meet the proposed patient care standards given the manpower and time constraints doctors face.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, I understand that doctors have very limited consultation time with their patients due to their workload.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With a short amount of time, doctors are expected to assess needs, comb through a vast amount of medical history information that may be available on the National Electronic Healthcare System, explain the situation and assist patients to make informed clinical decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Due to consult time constraints and possible differences in language and levels of understanding, patients may not be able to convey their concerns well enough to their doctors as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Doctors similarly may not be able to extract enough information to understand every aspect of the patient's concerns.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Time is also required to build understanding and to build confidence in the patient to undergo a recommended treatment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The stress of having to meet hospital KPIs measured in terms of consult time and manpower may also be overwhelming.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand some doctors fear what is reasonable to the court may in fact be humanly impossible to achieve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They also fear that such expectations can lead to further burnout amongst doctors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the calibration is not done well, this may tilt the balance towards doctors practicing defensive medicine while simultaneously managing consultation time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what additional support will be given to our doctors to allow them to meet these enhanced standards of advice that is required to be given to our patients?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will the doctor-patient ratio and consultation time be increased in public hospitals?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also provide assurance that practical circumstances of doctors will be taken into account when assessing the reasonableness of such advice?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He said, "Ultimately, we can do more harm if we assume that simply giving more information means the patient has more understanding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Giving more information could lead to less understanding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, no one benefits from this kind of defensive medicine because medical costs will go up and patients do not get the best advice from their doctors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Patient safety will be compromised." I hope we will provide a framework for a system which doctors can trust and that would be fair to the circumstances they face.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The system should take into account practical constraints, patient's preferences and the types of medical procedures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I declare my interest as a dispute resolution lawyer whose law firm advises on medical negligence cases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think many of the earlier speakers had focused on the Medical Registration (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will discuss a little bit about the Civil Law (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Civil Law Act is an old piece of legislation dating to 1909 and it provides rules covering a very wide range of discrete civil law issues that were not otherwise clear in the common law or in the legislation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes provisions giving the Courts power to administer equity and law at the same time, rules on the calculation of limitation periods for actions, administration of insolvent estates, rules on enforceability of gaming contracts, assessment of damages and contracts by minors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Each of these provisions addresses specific matters that were live issues at the time of legislation but have since become part of the rubric of our laws, co-existing with the other existing rules.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Today, a very specific rule relating to the test for issuing medical advice is joining this tapestry of other rules that form part of the Civil Law Act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the slightly older days when I was studying law in school, the classic "Bolam" test applied to every stage of the medical process, whether it was diagnosis, giving advice or treatment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This test was first articulated in the English case of Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee in 1957.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was essentially a test that if the doctor's actions were supported by a reasonable body of medical opinion, he would not be liable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was subsequently modified by a test called Bolitho, which said a doctor's decision must also be logically arrived at.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This test for medical negligence was commonly known as the Bolam-Bolitho test.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Typically, claims against doctors would proceed with parties engaging expert witnesses to assist the court and determine what this reasonable body of medical opinion was in relation to the actions in question.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Bolam test was devised under circumstances where it was assumed the doctor would play the most significant part in all decisions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, modern medical practice has very sensibly developed to give patients more choices in this process and in particular, for doctors to actually advise patients on treatment options available and the risk of each, while empowering patients to make the decision.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means significantly different considerations ought to apply when a doctor is giving advice as opposed to other matters such as diagnosis or treatment, where the patient may have no say.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If a patient is being diagnosed, that is very much in the doctor's hands.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If a patient is being treated, that is again in the doctor's hands.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But where a decision is being made, that is in fact a joint effort.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, where a patient has severe knee pain and a knee replacement may be an option, a doctor would likely advise the patient on a range of alternatives from surgery, including other ways of living with and managing the pain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The patient will ultimately make the decision on whether he prefers to go for surgery or deal with one of the other options.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If he opts for surgery, then of course the surgical process itself will be entirely in the doctor's hands.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The doctor would then be required to comply with the required test set out in "Bolam" to carry out that surgery.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, if the patient suffers from complications from that surgery even though the doctor took all steps that a reasonable body of medical opinion would support in the course of that surgery, then the doctor would not be liable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The decision for making that surgery, if made by a well-informed patient, would not be the doctor's fault.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was, in fact, the way the current test as we understood it developed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In fact, this development of the test was relatively recent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is what brings us to where we are today.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To me, this amendment is not so revolutionary and in some ways, to me, it looks like it is very consistent with the development of the law, including the developments by the courts in both England and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I note that the Civil Law Act is stated to replace the common law insofar as it is inconsistent but I think it may be helpful if the Minister could clarify how different this in fact is from the existing common law test, say, in Montgomery or Hii Chii Kok in relation to the giving of medical advice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although I think it is helpful to have this test set out specifically in legislation and also to have specific limbs stating exactly when and how the doctor should give information, to me, I think this is not a revolutionary change but rather a clarification of the common law position.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is always a challenge because in practical terms and I think many of my friends alluded to this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Doctors may get concerned about how much information they need to give and to what extent they have to advise patients of every single available option.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my understanding, case law is quite clear.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think if there is indeed a concern that defensive medicine is going to develop, then it is necessary to prevent that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my view, it is largely consistent with the common law and I think it places risk in the right places.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, risk for diagnosis and treatment is largely with doctors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And I think this legislation helps in that process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, for that reason I stand behind it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call for a break, Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon, would you like to make a clarification?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I was not preparing to make a speech during this debate, but Mr Murali made a reference to a sharing I had with him yesterday at the tea room.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And I thought it is useful for me to take this opportunity to share a larger context of what the conversation was because I think it adds texture to the debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For many in the House who may not be practising doctors – and I think I am going to say this as a doctor who has been dealing with informed consent for many complicated procedures, performing abdominal surgery – in the context of sharing, it is about when sharing more information can sometimes lead to paralysis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I think Mr Murali made the point; situations where a doctor may use therapeutic privilege to withhold information from patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I share this story of many old patients who may be afraid of going for surgery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And I think many of us who deal with elder patients will recognise that there is a subgroup of patients who are afraid of hearing the big "C" word – the word cancer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Sometimes, the word "cancer" would then force them into denial.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They will refuse treatment, to their own detriment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many family members in this context in Singapore which is very much an Asian-centric population where the patient relies a lot on their family members for a lot of social support and family members naturally will come to the doctor and say, "Please do not tell my mother or my father he has cancer".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I think it is in that context where the doctor himself may take on some professional risk as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But ultimately as doctors, we take the Hippocratic Oath seriously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our job is to first, be a patient advocate.
