speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Prior to being a Member of Parliament, I spent many years working as a civil servant in MOH.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I can attest to the fact that the practice of medicine is complex.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And many aspects may not be easily understood by the general public.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A comfortable and trusting relationship between a doctor and a patient is thus very important to bridge this knowledge gap.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Most people, especially the elderly, hold doctors in high regard.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, those who have elderly family members know how challenging it is to convince seniors to consult a doctor or even go for medical assessments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is worse if the patient is in a state of denial or lack insight.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But in recent years, trust between doctors and patients has been somewhat eroded by a spate of high-profile cases of negligence and unethical practices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There have also been reports of near misses and errors in the prescription of medicine.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, the younger generation when accompanying the elderly would often read up on the Internet beforehand.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thereafter, they may ask probing questions often to the chagrin of the doctors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This may then create simmering tensions between parties if there are disparities in treatment goals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Of course, the dilemma is how to provide information that is relevant to the patient to allow an informed decision.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Taking a step further, I hope the Ministry can support healthcare institutions, especially those frequently used by our seniors, to reduce communication barriers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This person must be able to facilitate the flow of information between the doctors and patients who can understand only dialects or local languages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When complex terms are delivered in one’s own language, it can reduce the unease the patient may face at a doctor’s consult.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also helps to improve the doctor-patient relationship.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is heartening to read that in Changi General Hospital they were experimenting with i-COMM, an AI to produce communication apps for dialects and mother tongues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can surely leverage more on technology to help us in this endeavour.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another crucial factor to improve good communication is for doctors to consider the patient’s profile when obtaining informed consent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An example would be elderly patients who may not have completed their formal education.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I see many of such seniors in Yio Chu Kang today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may require an approach where doctors exercise professional judgement by taking into account the benefits, limitations and risks relevant to them and translating that into recommendations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, a younger, educated and well-informed patient may prefer a more detailed description of the benefits, limitations and risks to be explained to them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With this knowledge, they will then make their own decision and assessment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In case of suspected misconduct, patients should not have to face unduly onerous rules to lodge a complaint or request an investigation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, I am against families or patients who abuse the professional disciplinary process when their informed choice of treatment did not give the desired outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A balance needs to be struck where a patient has access to justice under a robust system, yet does not abuse the process and take up resources that can be better deployed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And how will this timeline affect any current backlog of cases?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will also be useful if the Minister can share with us plans to clear the backlog.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, how can we simplify the process so that it would not be so onerous that it would turn away a complainant from highlighting dangerous practice?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note that cost orders may be imposed if a complaint is found to be frivolous.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This should be made known to a complainant, before he proceeds with his action.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I can personally attest to the benefits and advantages of mediation, having served as a mediator in the Community Mediation Centre at MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should ideally keep the cost of mediation affordable for patients to take up this route.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The ease and relative advantages of mediation should be emphasised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Often, medical disputes arise due to simple miscommunication.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mediation can help to avoid an ugly law suit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Tapping on the Singapore Mediation Centre or SMC is a good option as the SMC already has expertise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mediators from the SMC could benefit from training to equip them with knowledge and sensitivities to handle medical-related disputes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I understand that MOHH likewise has a Healthcare Mediation Scheme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Whilst the fractured relationship rarely fully heals, I know for a fact that mediation goes some way in allowing parties to talk face to face and rebuild trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe it is timely that we address all the above issues so that we can further grow the mutual respect between the patient and the doctor in our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And as more patients face not one, but multiple conditions interacting with each other in complex ways on the one hand and as therapies become more advanced on the other, the healthcare decisions that doctors have to make will only become more complex.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, this debate about regulating the professional and ethical practice of medicine in our society is not taking place in a static context, but in an operating environment that will become more demanding and more complex going forward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is therefore a timely debate and one that we must get right, because the stakes are high and will only get higher.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Against this backdrop, we must guard zealously against defensive medicine, because it is bad for everyone.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The US Congress' Office of Technology Assessment defines defensive medicine as occurring when, and I quote, "doctors order tests, procedures or visits, or avoid high-risk patients or procedures, primarily to reduce their exposure to malpractice liability." This was published in 1994.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Now, as an example of defensive medicine and this is anecdotal, in one hospital in Singapore, there is a large number of a certain scan that is ordered each year to look for a particular condition of the lungs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, doctors at the hospital are frequently ordering the scan and a rather expensive one at that, but rarely, finding anything adverse.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is a specific type of behaviour in defensive medicine known as assurance behaviour.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Minister, in his Second Reading speech just now spoke about a study showing avoidance behaviour, that is when doctors do not order a test when it is appropriate to do so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Assurance behaviour is the opposite, when doctors order tests when it is not entirely appropriate.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And yes, it seems to be happening here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In 2017, a major paper published in the Lancet presents compelling evidence on the overuse of medical services around the world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, there is overuse of medication, the best-documented example being the inappropriate use of antibiotics.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Second, there is overuse of screening tests, even for cervical and breast cancers, and screening colonoscopy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Now, the study observes that the harm to patients caused by overuse can be physical, in the form of side effects and complications, financial and psychological.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The paper concludes that, and I quote, "The provision of medical services that are more likely to cause harm than good is a global problem that afflicts rich and poor countries alike." Sir, the amendments in these Bills have been made amidst a significant level of disquiet in the medical profession.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The high-profile decisions last year, around specific issues of informed consent and patient confidentiality, had brought this disquiet to the fore, but I think it stemmed from a broader uncertainty about standards of care and a general gap in confidence in the professional disciplinary process and its outcomes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Members before me have spoken on the merits of specific amendments and I will not belabour these.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think the amendments, as well as the non-legislative measures, as a whole, are decisive and better grounded in practice realities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I hope this would help restore trust between doctors and the regulatory system and arrest the risk of us sliding further towards defensive medicine, to the detriment of both patients and professionals.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As the hon Member Dr Tan Wu Meng puts it, we must help doctors to help patients, because this is the way to help both doctors and patients.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That said, we must avoid swinging to the other extreme, where patients without medical training or deep resources are left to feel like their access to justice in this system has been compromised.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: When something goes wrong, we must have a system that works for both patient and doctor.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, for instance, while I welcome the proposal for an Inquiry Committee to act as a first and efficient level of triage for the merits of a complaint, prima facie, complete facts will become crucial for the Committee to effectively perform its intended function.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I therefore urge the Ministry to look into providing resources to guide lay complainants through the filing process, especially in providing supporting documents and other evidence.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is a key detail in implementation that would safeguard patient welfare.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But while we strike that fine balance at a system that works for both doctor and patient, ultimately, the panacea against defensive medicine cannot be about enhancing a system of recourse and justice for times when something goes wrong.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Rather, our surest inoculation against defensive medicine must be that broad public confidence that in our system, things would by and large, and almost always, go right.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: More to the point, when I am the patient, I must feel that things would go right, for me.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Objectively, this must mean that our system has high standards of quality and safety.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng has spoken about the roles of both the individual and the system to achieve these.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But more viscerally, this is also about the deep human-to-human relationship between patient and doctor.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is why we talk in terms of care, instead of just treating an illness.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is why we talk in terms of the experience, instead of just a consultation or a procedure.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And this is why there is a whole emerging field on empathy in medical education – systematically teaching doctors about kindness and compassion.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is why a doctor's "bedside manners" matter so much to us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, at the University of Texas at Austin, their Medical School and the College of Fine Arts have joined forces to form a Design Institute for Health.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is their way to deliberately bring design sensibilities into healthcare, because design is ultimately about addressing human needs, and they have recognised that healthcare is first and foremost about the human relationship.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It goes well beyond a transaction, or a delivery of service.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And if we think about it, our healthcare system is essentially the sum of millions of these relationships, exchanging value on a daily basis and at a micro-level.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, the system can only work effectively and sustainably when these relationships are thriving, on the basis of a high level of trust.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, when all is said and done, it is time to double down on trust.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is time to double down on both the human relationships and the professional quality in our system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Amongst hospital management teams here, there is a common saying: we aspire to provide "care that is good enough for my mother".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And then someone said, perhaps it should be care that is good enough for my mother-in-law.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Well, I shall leave it to Members to mull over the material differences.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But it is a case of differences but same same.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Beyond legislation and policy, institutions on the ground are working relentlessly at high quality and quality relationships, creating care that is good enough for our own loved ones.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Trust is our ballast for a sustainable and effective system to secure our healthcare future and meet the many complex challenges ahead.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: First, let me just begin by declaring my interest as a member of the medical profession.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The amendments are timely as there is a need to enhance the legislative processes to protect patients’ rights as well as to preserve the trust between the doctors and the patient.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: About 20 cases or about 10% of these complaints are categorised under “No/Inappropriate or Inadequate Informed consent”.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While the trend is stable now, we are deeply concerned that cases may increase in light of the experience overseas.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Allow me just briefly to share with you what happened in UK, the National Health System or NHS has reported in 2015 that a study found that negligence claims against NHS doctors due to failure to inform patients before they consent to procedures have spiralled upwards since the landmark legal ruling in 2015.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This research was done by Queen Mary University of London, found that while the rate of other claims has remained steady, cases relating to consent have risen fourfold overall since March 2015 – where failure to inform was added as a contributory claim, the rise was nearly tenfold.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As a background, let me share that this change follows a landmark Supreme Court judgment – known as Montgomery judgment – that changes the legal test for determining what is sufficient disclosure before consent is given to treatment, by moving away from asking what a reasonable doctor would warn and asking instead to what a reasonable patient would expect to know.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It would be relevant to add to my understanding that even the wisdom in the Montgomery case now is an issue being debated in the legal circles.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The key is how is a doctor to strike a balance between an information overload for the patient versus too little information.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With all due respect to all our patients, they are all different.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some may not understand the choices before them, especially where the choices are scientifically complex.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And doctors would only be adding to emotional burden of the patients, causing alarm and confusion unnecessarily.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Hence, the materiality of information is a real challenge.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Of course, the patient could have his family members or her family members to explain to him or her and hopefully there is no loss of critical information in the course of the communication.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For many healthcare practitioners, working with seniors and foreign patients who do not speak any of our four national languages poses one of the greatest challenges.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In a small clinical set-up, there is simply a shortage of resources with the necessary interpreting skills as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In cases of complications as a result of lack of informed consent, who would be liable?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The doctor for failing to obtain the consent, or the interpreter for misinterpreting?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Apart from doctors, patients too would have a responsibility to share more about their personal health, for example, their health history and habits which in a consultation in the presence of family members the patient may not find it convenient to share their full disclosure to the doctors.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With increasing medical litigation, the medical indemnity insurance premium paid by doctors are also rising exponentially year after year.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In US, the annual medical indemnity insurance premium paid by practising obstetricians last year can be as high as a quarter of US$1 million per year.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many of the US O&G specialists gave up practising obstetrics simply because they just find that their earnings are not enough to cover the premiums or the risk being sued is too high to bear.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I hope in Singapore, we will not move in that direction.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If we do, ultimately the consumers, our patients, will bear the cost.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the last two years, I and a few Members of Parliament brought up in this Chamber the inappropriately harsh penalties given to doctors by Singapore Medical Council's Disciplinary Tribunal and we were concerned with the rising trend.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This will lead to defensive medicine if left unchecked and a further escalation of medical costs to all of us.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This amendment will affirm our patient’s rights and at the same time give some clarity and assurance to our medical fraternity on a fair and expeditious system that handles medical complaints by SMC.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Number one, the increase in cost and resources to SMC.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The setting up of more layers to handle public complaints will require more manpower and resources.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can MOH give more grant to SMC to offset the increase in cost?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The changes also call for more doctors to come forward to serve on SMC’s committees.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Currently, how many doctors are serving on the SMC to handle public complaints?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How many more doctors will be required with this new proposal?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What plans do MOH have to increase the number of doctors serving in these committees and how do you attract them?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With increasing cost involved, will SMC consider levying a small administrative fee for public to file their complaint?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: By charging a small fee, it may also deter frivolous complaints too.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I know for now MOH is not considering leveraging an administrative fee for public who file complaints but I hope MOH will consider this later?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In the example given, a patient with history of eczema had skin complications after undergoing an orthopaedic surgery.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Is there a time bar for the medical records in this example?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am supportive to have mediation as a mechanism to resolve some of these complaints before the case is being escalated to the Disciplinary Tribunal or the Courts.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For mediation suggested in this amendment, is it mandatory?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This new committee would sift through at first level, those frivolous and vexatious complaints before they even reach the Complaints Committee.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Inquiry Committee would thus be able to either dismiss a complaint, issue a letter of advice or refer the matter to the Complaints Committee and also to refer for mediation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Inquiry Committee would also be able to refer the matter to mediation before making these orders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All of these measures are necessary and welcomed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They balance both the interests of the patient or the family, usually the complainant, and that of the doctor being complained of.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I draw parallels between this Inquiry Committee and that of the Review Committee of the Law Society of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can draw lessons from similar amendments to the Legal Profession Act or LPA.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Those amendments were back in 2001 which had introduced a Review Committee.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The function of the Review Committee in the LPA is also to review each complaint and dismiss those that are "frivolous, vexatious, misconceived or lacking in substance".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In a 2018 Court of Appeal case Re Nalpon, Zero Geraldo   SGCA 71, the decision of a Review Committee in the LPA was challenged by way of a judicial review.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The case involved a complaint against lawyers by another lawyer.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The complainant challenged the decision of the Review Committee, saying that it had made its decision in just seven days, provided only a brief statement of its decision and did not even call the complainant or the lawyers that was the subject of his complaint to provide any further information or clarification.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although the judicial review challenge ultimately failed before the Court, the case highlighted the risk of protracted litigation if the first stage of the Review Committee and, in this case, the Inquiry Committee does not sufficiently manage or meet with the complaint's expectations, especially in those cases involving lay persons and grieving families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will help to conclude the matter efficiently, but for complainants, especially the families, they need closure sooner rather than later.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A couple of weeks ago, a resident informed me that her pregnant sister-in-law suffered severe bleeding while under the care of a hospital.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She delivered her baby prematurely and because of some complications, the baby now suffers from permanent brain damage.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are a young working couple and that was their firstborn.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are now questioning the standard of care that they were given.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the past month, I attended a wake of a deceased elderly parent of a long-time resident of mine and volunteer.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The daughter questioned whether early detection and intervention by a particular doctor would have saved her mother’s life.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These are questions that families in grief are grappling with.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These families may or may not probe further or proceed on in their actions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But if they do, then this system of regulating the complaints against doctors and the medical profession must not only be efficient but it also must be humane in the way it explains the true situation and circumstances to the families in grief.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill thus must be seen in the light of its true intentions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not intended to shield doctors against complaints but it is to balance all interests and ensure protection and adequate recourse for patients and families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In 2011, a close relative suffered complications after surgery and passed away in the hospital.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Her parents had not seen her graduate yet.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She had a full life ahead of her.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Naturally, in a time of tragedy and loss, the parents sought answers to explain their loss by questioning the system and the treating doctors and hospital.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That process took more than two years, which ultimately found that there was no wrongdoing or negligence by the treating doctors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although there was finality to the process, the sheer duration did not give the family any closure nor heal any wounds.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nothing can beguile parents from a loss of a child so overwhelming or assuage the anguish of their bereavement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is thus important to quicken the complaint process and disciplinary procedure, which is what this Bill aims to do so as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am heartened that a legal advisory unit will be set up to support and advise the Inquiry Committee.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With greater medical knowledge and public awareness and increasingly complex medical situations, there would be more cases in which doctors may be faced with complaints.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think he has given a very vivid explanation of why doctors need to feel that they are able to take some risk with the patient, able to advance the patient's interests in the best way that they know how to do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Knowing the information that they have, making the judgement that they do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in some ways, trying to make the best decision and guide the patient towards that best decision sometimes does require the doctor to take a position – to exercise some degree of therapeutic privilege and to assess the kind of information that ought to be appropriate for not just this kind of injury and this kind of outcome but for this kind of patient and their family and overall, not losing sight of the end outcome.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would dare say that the majority of doctors want to be in that position where they do not have to look over their shoulder, they do not have to worry about what the patient might say and worry first about whether or not they have given everything to the patient based on the textbook.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think that is really an illustration of why the practice of medicine is truly an art and is not a science.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is an inexact art to begin with.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a judgement call in every sense of the word.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is in that context that we start with the proposition that we do not want to place labels on the test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is why Mr Pillai is right that in this Bill, we have deliberately stayed away from putting that label on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yes, it was discussed in the context of the previous decisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is the terminology that has been used.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The work group has also used that terminology, but we have chosen to make sure that we stay away from it – as far as we can, to advance it as a common denominator of benefiting the patient and the doctor together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What do we see as the value of making this change?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Earlier on, Mr Xie, Dr Lim Wee Kiak had talked about what the position was in the UK post-Montgomery, and I think there is a lesson to be learned there as well – the number of cases not just post-Montgomery but in respect of informed consent post-Montgomery.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But look at the position in Singapore based on cases filed with the SMC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That was in the year around the period of time when the Lim Lian Arn DT or Disciplinary Tribunal was decided.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Pillai's point – and I get your point that perhaps if it is just a perception, why not we just deal with the perception.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is a sign that we do need to do something about it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We therefore look at the test as trying to give doctors that degree of assurance when they first walk into a consultation room.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The test starts with, as a matter of philosophy, what would my peers do in that situation?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A peer might be a peer like Dr Koh's peers, who would decide that in such a situation, there is something to be gained by exercising therapeutic privilege.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not something that patients easily understand if you look at it from the patient's perspective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I want to make one other observation, which is that in every single case where the patient's perspective is called into question and you have to assess what is the patient's perspective – whether it is a quasi-criminal case when it is before the Disciplinary Tribunal or DT, or whether it is a civil liability case – at that juncture, when you are assessing and talking about the patient's perspective, there is already an adverse issue between the patient and the doctor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The claim has already been made or the complaint has already been made.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is why you are looking at the patient's perspective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The patient's perspective is going to be very different.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if you are a doctor, you think about walking into a room.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You think about the therapeutic privilege that perhaps Dr Koh might think about, and then worry about whether or not at some stage downstream – not in the light of this fairly amicable discussion in the consultation room today – but you think about what might happen if you start the inquiry as, "What would that patient in that particular perspective want to know?" Then, I think the outcome might well be very different or at least perceived to be very different.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is going to be a tangible impact on the way you conduct yourself as a doctor.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We therefore want philosophically to start with giving the doctors the assurance that when you walk into a room with a typical patient, average patient, this is what the practice of peer professionals would do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As long as you conform with that as a starting point, that is your baseline.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned earlier in my speech, it is the baseline standard.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Well, we also want to work with the professional bodies like Academy of Medicine of Singapore or AMS.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want to work with them to ensure that as far as they are concerned, for some of these more standard procedures, there is a benchmark that can be used to educate and inform doctors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Earlier on, a Member said: let us not wait until these cases are decided by the Court, because by that time, it is too late – at least for that case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want to proactively look at what we can do, working with the fraternity to help the fraternity understand this better.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also want to amend the ECEG as I said earlier on to give better guidance to doctors on how these guidelines are to be applied.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Pritam Singh's point about Recommendation 3 in the work group's report – yes, that is something that we will continue to look at, put in place and with due course, to have sufficient level of guidance for the medical fraternity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Going back to this test, we therefore start with, "What would my peers do in a typical consultation like this?" But we graft onto it what we regard as giving primacy to the patient's inquiries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you go in and you do not say anything, we have some rules that set out what a doctor has to reasonably ascertain.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That still has to be addressed by the doctor to their satisfaction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if I am a doctor and you ask me about a concern that is otherwise not within the radar of the peer professional opinion, I still have to address it, I still have to get my information to you correctly on what is the risk for this particular type of very small injury, which may not be material to many other people but to this patient, it is.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is my patient, I have to address it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is how we strike that balance between certain starting points for doctors, but also taking into account patient autonomy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On this second question about what might be reasonably looked at and what is material.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Dr Lim's point, we do not need to look at all the medical records, all the microfiches, all the scans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you ask me today, standing here, can we come up with a formula for what is reasonable, I think that is not possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would not rule it out but the less likely it is.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It probably would have been superseded by something else.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is really designed with the illustrations to give some degree of fluidity and some flexibility to look at the particular situation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With this framework, and I think Mr Vikram Nair also said, actually this is something that is very familiar territory.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Not every detail needs to be given and within this framework, I think most doctors, if not, at least the lawyers would know, what is the peer opinion?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Who would qualify as a good, decent peer?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What is an opinion that is logical, defensible, internally consistent?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Then, you graft onto it – what did the patient ask or if the patient did not ask, what is reasonable to derive from the information before you?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is how we see the test operating.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In some ways, to answer Dr Tan's point, we had to put out legislation to deal with this partly because we saw this was how it was going.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We looked at the numbers that have been cited by myself and Members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We looked at observations of the work group.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We understand where this is going and we understand that it might be a perception and it might well even be wrong.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But that is the way in which the industry is reacting to it and I think it behooves us to do something about it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is why these amendments have been offered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is a fair concern and the point is taken.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Anything that has got to do with putting on more workload and the workload then perhaps undermining the quality of care is something that MOH would be concerned about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I would like to assure Members about that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I would also like to say that we need to frame a test now which best promotes the doctor-patient relationship, gives that relationship the best chance of having a good interactive discourse that promotes the best outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yes, there might be an increase in workload – although I do have something to say about that in a moment – but that ought not to be the starting point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That should not drive the way we define or formulate this test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We may have to find ways to work around it, to put better resources in public hospitals or polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But, as in designing the Civil Law Act test, I think we must first focus, and perhaps only focus, on what is good for the patient and doctor in that relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Anecdotally, I also do not see this formulation adding more to the current status quo.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It might add more to what might have been the old Bolam test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, if anything, you take that back 10 to 15 years, the numbers actually have come down.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But that said, I appreciate the point made by both Mr Pritam Singh as well as Dr Tan Wu Meng about looking after the systemic issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked what might be an idiosyncratic reason.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I will just briefly mention that an idiosyncratic reason is just a reason that is peculiar to that patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It may not be relevant or material to many other patients or most other patients or, in fact, maybe even any other patient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But if to that patient it is, and he has asked the question about it, then the doctor is required to address those concerns.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pritam Singh also asked what do we do with a multi-disciplinary team setting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would just like to say that, actually, in today's context, most care is given in that setting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you go to a polyclinic, there is a team that looks after you.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you go to a PHI, a public hospital, there is also a team that looks after you.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the law actually takes that into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The law does not require that only one doctor, the leading doctor, takes the consent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The law does accept that any member of the team can take the consent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But, obviously, the requirements of the consent-taking has to be fulfilled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Pritam Singh's point that we must look at this more frequently and regularly, we agree.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is actually quite a baseline consideration, given that medical technology innovation is changing, evolving, and we do want to ensure that our system that looks after discipline has the public interest of the patients at heart, is constantly updated and kept updated with technological progress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked several questions, one of which was in relation to the cases that can go directly to a DT.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: He asked why the SMC was allowed to retain some discretion in doing that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The answer to that is that it depends on the nature of the case and it gives the SMC some degree of latitude in terms of assessing the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The SMC themselves will then play a more proactive role in reviewing and determining whether these cases ought to be directed to the DT straightaway.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the interim orders and the fact that the interim orders committees have a wide remit to determine what is necessary for the protection of members of the public or otherwise in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is put in that form so that it can allow the IOC to take into account a broad spectrum of matters, including how it affects public interest, when it might affect public interest and the kind of occasions or risk factors that a doctor is exposed to in any given scenario and, therefore, tailor the way in which the IOC orders are sought accordingly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, these were the two recent cases, by way of examples, to assure Members that this is not going to be used at a very low threshold.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Mr Louis Ng asked about the composition of non-SMC members currently at the Complaints Panel, and the resourcing issues that we will have to address post-passing of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That, in part, also answers Mr Leon Perera's point about the way in which we will engage patient advocacy groups.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Looking at these numbers, the representation by lay persons, or rather non-doctors, is not small and not insignificant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the role they play directly in the process in the Complaints Committee, in fact, in several other committees that are set up in the SMC, that takes into account the non-medical, non-doctor input as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Obviously, we look at the volume of cases to determine whether or not that will be sufficient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But looking at the statistics, the numbers and what we forecast, these are the numbers that we intend to start with once the Bill is operationalised and then we can decide whether we want to move up thereafter.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the IC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The IC will share the reasons, as I have outlined in my opening speech, for its decision, so that members of the public who have complained and the complaint is being dismissed by the IC will be aware not only of the decision but also of the reasons for the IC reaching that view.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason for the IC is that it needs to act as a stronger filter.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Today, yes, we have 6% to 7% of cases that are filtered away from that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But let me cite the Lim Lian Arn example to Members.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In Lim Lian Arn, the Court of Three Judges felt that there was a miscarriage of justice and one of the factors they looked at was to analyse the complaint and they formed the view that even if the complaint was taken in its extreme, that means, you accept every fact set out by the complainant as correct and true, that still does not amount to professional misconduct.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And there was a very detailed analysis by the Chief Justice in that case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And those are precisely the type of cases that we want to be able to filter at the IC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The IC, together with legal resources, we feel will be better equipped to look at these cases, apply the law to these cases early and upfront, rather than, as in the case of Dr Lim's case, have the case travel through the system for a good four or five years, using up resources in that period of time, only to be thrown out at the hearing of final reckoning, at the last stage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, that is what we want to do – to move the decision-making, move the resourcing upfront, and have that dealt with as early as we can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Louis Ng asked for some timelines and also about some resourcing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we have the remainder of the last quarter of 2019 cases standing, and then we are into 2020 cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over the last two years or so, the SMC had worked very hard and managed to resolve many of these cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have explained to members, this new regime will not be able to apply to existing cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the existing cases still have to follow the current track and the current timelines.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Cases filed once this Bill is in force will enjoy the new track.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Ang Wei Neng and Dr Lim Wee Kiak are all obviously very concerned about what Minister Gan might have to do to ask Deputy Prime Minister Heng, seated next to him now, for additional resources.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I wanted to say that these are changes that we have made which we believe will enhance the system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You either spend on the system having a case travel through like I have explained in Dr Lim's case and incur a lot of resources and, at the same time, you do not really get any good outcomes as far as the doctor or the patient is concerned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Rather, we think resources are better spent putting upfront legal resources, mediation resources and a good filtering system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, yes, that requires manpower and also resources.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some Members are concerned whether we will have sufficient resources to support the new structure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason for this is because the grants have been given to SMC to look at setting up these structures to look at redeploying what we have currently used, by way of resources, to deal with the cases which have taken four, five years or so to deal with but applying them upfront.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we feel we can manage with the current resources.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If not, we can top it up with some more, and I think Minister Gan will have to approach the Deputy Prime Minister for that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the idea is to be cost-neutral as far as possible because we believe that this is in a public interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a system meant to safeguard patient welfare, public interest and public confidence in the system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is why, like Dr Lim Wee Kiak had suggested, we also do not want to put a financial bar in front of every complainant before you can make a complaint to the SMC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That was something that was actually canvassed quite robustly at many of the town halls to put a fee upfront before a complainant can make a complaint.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we studied it and we decided, as did the work group, that we did not want, and it was against public interest, to put a financial bar to patients to file a complaint.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Instead, we decided that we will empower the CCs and the DTs to grant costs in the appropriate cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My colleagues, who are lawyers in this House, will know that that is used very sparingly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The power does exist in the Legal Profession Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is used very sparingly and, really, as a measure of last resort to ensure that these frivolous vexatious claims do not continue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Leon Perera supported the Bill and said that it is in the right directions, which I appreciate, and also raised several suggestions for us to consider.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think he had about 10 or 12 suggestions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I cannot cover them all here in today's response.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of the time bar and the limitation period, why was there a difference?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reason is because when we have a complaint, as I have mentioned just now, about a doctor's conduct, this is an issue of public interest in itself because we are talking about upholding standards and confidence in the way in which doctors give treatment to patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, compared to a civil or commercial time bar where you are locked out from making a monetary claim, for example, or a claim for land, you are locked out after six years or such other period as the time limitation might prescribe.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those come on a very different footing from trying to look at complaints or entertain complaints outside of the time bar when you are talking about upholding public interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, in terms of the certified training, I think I have covered part of it in my response to Mr Singh's suggestion of Recommendation 3.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a very significant plank of what we have proposed here, as you have heard me saying.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But that should also be taken in conjunction with the sentencing guidelines that have now been issued.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also want to remind Members that we have a legal unit that will support each of the committees across the spectrum of when they review the cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Perera is right that there are already training programmes that are on-going now today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am told that they have been fairly well attended until there was a break during the last few months because of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But there has also been specific training not just for the members of the CC and the DT because they require more specialist training, but also encouraging doctors, as a whole, even if you are not involved in the CC or the DT, to have at least some basic knowledge of medico-legal principles.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think that overall, with time, would help the appreciation of the standard of care, would help in appreciation of how doctors are to interact with their patients.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Perera talked about whether we could recognise the support and remunerate persons who sit in in these Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But it is also very difficult, as I think Mr Perera also noted, to quantify the amount of remuneration to give.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When you are designing a system that is meant to be a self-regulating system, then people within that system must step forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I heard Dr Lim Wee Kiak say that we must encourage more members to come forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This system is really only sustainable if the best, the most experienced, those who can afford the time and even those who cannot afford the time, should step forward and serve in some capacity in the CCs, in the DTs, in the RCs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And it is not just because of the honorarium or the financial compensation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And to borrow a phrase from my colleague, "No one has a monopoly over good suggestions".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we welcome suggestions even after the Bill might be passed.
